text:
Benjamin Netanyahu received a direct warning that Hamas was planning a major attack in the run-up to 7 October 2023 but failed to act, an Israeli newspaper has alleged. 

The investigation, published by Haaretz on Tuesday, claims that UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed told the Israeli prime minister by phone that the armed group was “preparing for a major event”. 

Netanyahu did not tell intelligence and military leaders about the conversation, according to the report, which cites unnamed senior foreign sources and a close adviser to bin Zayed who was present on the call. 

Israeli intelligence officials were, however, made aware of Hamas’ plans for an attack, according to the investigation: then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar warned Israel himself via an intermediary. 

Netanyahu’s office called the claim an “absolute lie” and denied that he had a call with the Emirati leader around that time or received any warning. The office of bin Zayed did not respond to a request for comment from Haaretz.

After growing frustrated with stalled negotiations aimed at lifting Israel’s illegal blockade on Gaza, Sinwar reportedly told the mediator to “convey a message” to the Israeli side. He said: “I am preparing the mother of all surprises. A terrifying operation. Something extraordinary." 

On 15 September, both the mediator and bin Zayed’s advisor relayed the message to Shin Bet, Israel’s internal intelligence service, the report alleges. Ex-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and ex-IDF chief of staff Herzl Halevi said they were not informed of a warning from the president of the UAE.   

An anonymous intelligence official quoted by Haaretz speculated that Sinwar sent the warning to “pressure” Israel into reaching a deal, or else as a tactic to assess the readiness of the Israel Defense Forces. 

It has previously been reported that Egyptian officials warned Israel just days before 7 October that “something catastrophic” was about to happen.

In the wake of the attacks, Haaretz reports, Hamas was willing to unconditionally release all civilian captives, or at least all those below the age of 18 and over 50. Further offers followed, but Netanyahu’s government refused to engage, sources said.

text:
The most successful pirate in history was a Chinese woman named Ching Shih.

At the beginning of the 19th century, Ching Shih worked as a prostitute aboard a floating brothel known as a “Flower Boat” — a vessel filled with women. Sailing through the South China Sea, these establishments offered not only sexual services but also theatrical performances. In other words, they provided entertainment for both body and soul.

At the age of 26, Ching Shih found the man of her life — possibly among her clients. His name was Zheng Yi, and he was a pirate, one of the most dangerous sea raiders in southern China, controlling a significant part of the region’s waters. But before marrying him, the clever Ching Shih reportedly set a condition: she would be his loyal wife, but he would allow her to share power over his fleet.

For the time, the idea of a woman ruling an army of thousands alongside a man was extraordinary, but the pirate world did not necessarily follow the conventions of life on land. Customs were different. For example, since the couple had no children of their own, they adopted a young fisherman named Zhang Baozai.

Their marriage did not last long. After several years, Zheng Yi died. Ching Shih then moved quickly to secure control over the pirate confederation. At the height of its power, the organization commanded hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of pirates — an enormous maritime force.

Ching Shih formed a close personal and political partnership with the young Zhang Baozai, her late husband’s adopted son. He eventually became her lover and later her husband. Some accounts suggest that the nature of Zhang’s relationship with Zheng Yi and Ching Shih may have been more complicated than the traditional description of him simply as their adopted son.

Aboard the ships under Ching Shih’s influence, discipline was brutal. It was one of the few ways to control such an enormous force. Together with Zhang Baozai, she enforced a strict code of conduct. Disobeying orders could be punishable by death. Stealing from the common treasury was severely punished, as was the sexual abuse of female captives. Some captured women were released, while others became wives or partners of pirates.

Ching Shih and her allies proved remarkably successful at uniting previously competing pirate fleets into a huge confederation.

The pirate organizations of the 18th and early 19th centuries were not always merely scattered gangs hunted by the authorities. Some became powerful political and military forces with their own territories, economic networks, hierarchies, traditions, and codes of law.

Zhang Baozai soon became one of the confederation’s most important commanders, inspiring both fear and respect among his men.

The Qing government could not tolerate such a powerful force operating along China’s coast. Beginning in 1808, imperial forces launched major attempts to destroy the pirate confederation. But defeating it proved extraordinarily difficult, and government forces suffered humiliating setbacks.

Over the following years, Ching Shih’s pirates faced not only rival pirate groups and Qing forces but also pressure involving Portuguese naval forces. Although the pirate confederation gradually weakened, destroying it outright remained extremely difficult.

Eventually, the Qing authorities chose negotiation over annihilation.

In 1810, Ching Shih accepted an amnesty. Most remarkably, she managed to leave piracy without suffering the fate that awaited so many other famous pirates. Zhang Baozai surrendered as well and later entered government service.

The couple subsequently had a son. Zhang Baozai died years later, leaving Ching Shih a widow once again.

She eventually settled in Guangzhou, where later accounts say she operated a gambling establishment. Stories also associate her later business activities with the opium trade.

Ching Shih died in 1844, reportedly at about 69 years old.

text:
'The time has come for global isolation.'

 'There is no need to say much more. We have heard it all by now and from all parties. We all know what is going on—it can’t be “occupied territory” if the land is your own. 

As a result, everyone else is either an enemy, a “self-hater,” or both. If we have to mask annexation, so be it. In any case, there is no need to take responsibility for the suffering inflicted on the other party because we have convinced ourselves that the other party does not exist.      

Thus thuggishness, jingoism, racist rhetoric, and sectarianism. Thus every two or three years, an all-out, asymmetrical assault against a population entrapped in an open-air prison.      

We each know why they do what they do—the army, the police, the settlers, the pilots of bombing raids, the zealots, and the cohort of international Pharisees and their mandatory righteousness, starting with the United States of America.  

We all know what is going on: by any means necessary, they must be purged from the land.  I am willing to bet on the following:      

▪️ In Palestine, it would be hard to find one single person who has not lost someone—a member of the family, a friend, a close relative, a neighbor.        

▪️It would be hard to find one single person who is unaware of what “collateral damage” is all about.      

▪️It is worse than the South African Bantustans.  To be sure, it is not apartheid, South African style. It is far more lethal. It looks like high-tech Jim Crow-cum-apartheid.  

The refusal of citizenship to those who are not like us. Encirclement. Never enough land taken. It is all a gigantic mess. Rage, resentment, and despair. The melding of strength, victimhood, and a supremacist complex. 

No wonder even the  Europeans are now threatening Israel with sanctions.  Israel is entitled to live in peace. But Israel will be safeguarded only by peace in a confederal arrangement that recognizes reciprocal residency if not citizenship.  

The occupation of Palestine is the biggest moral scandal of our times, one of the most dehumanizing ordeals of the century we have just entered, and the biggest act of cowardice of the last half-century.    

And since all they are willing to offer is a fight to the finish, since what they are willing to do is to go all the way—carnage, destruction, incremental extermination—the time has come for global isolation.'  

Achille Mbembe's foreword to 'Apartheid Israel: The Politics of an Analogy', a book where eighteen scholars of Africa reflect on the similarities and differences between Apartheid South Africa and Apartheid Israel (2015).

text:
Uganda's oil projects, including Tilenga by @TotalEnergiesUG  and Kingfisher by @CNOOCUgandaLtd  plus the @EACOP_  pipeline, are advancing toward first exports with the recent unveiling of the "Pearl Sweet" crude blend, amid drilling in ecologically sensitive areas like Murchison Falls National Park.

Environmentally, activities risk wildlife displacement causing human-elephant conflicts, threats to wetlands and Lake Albert fisheries, potential spills affecting the Nile headwaters, and lifetime emissions around 379 million tons of CO2.

Politically, the developments involve major foreign investment, promises of jobs and revenue for Uganda's economy, but have led to documented community displacements, compensation disputes, and international scrutiny over land rights and governance.
EACOP (the East African Crude Oil Pipeline) and the linked @TIlenga  and Kingfisher oilfields have caused both physical relocation of homes and much larger economic displacement through loss of farmland and access. Official project figures and community/NGO reports differ on scale and outcomes.

Project documents and company updates put EACOP-affected households at roughly 3,650–3,760 in Uganda and about 9,900 in Tanzania (around 13,700 households total). Most of those lose only a strip of land for the 30-metre corridor rather than their house. Physically displaced households—those who lost a dwelling—are far fewer: about 200 in Uganda and 340 in Tanzania. Tilenga separately affected nearly 5,000 households in Buliisa, Hoima and Kikuube, with a few hundred primary residences rebuilt. Broader counts that include everyone who lost any land or access sometimes reach 100,000 individuals across both countries.

Companies report that more than 99 percent of compensation agreements have been signed and paid, and that replacement houses have been handed over. People were offered cash or a project-built house. Many who took cash later said the amounts were too low to buy equivalent land because prices rose after the project was announced, and that they received little independent legal advice. Those who took houses have described uniform, small dwellings that do not match previous household size, plus resettlement sites that lack nearby water, markets or clinics. Harvests and reported incomes often fell after the move.

Kingfisher, operated by CNOOC, has drawn sharper allegations: forced evictions by security forces, land deals routed through a communal association rather than individual households, missing or unpublished resettlement plans, and fishing communities evicted near Lake Albert with incomplete compensation. Some pastoralist families evicted earlier (around 2010) say they are still waiting. Gender effects appear in several studies: compensation was often paid to men, leaving women without land or cash. Grave relocations and loss of grazing land have also disrupted cultural practices, especially among pastoralist groups in Tanzania.
The net picture is a mix of completed paperwork and persistent livelihood gaps. Most affected people are smallholder farmers; once land is taken or fragmented, restoring previous income and food security has been uneven even where payments were made.
The oil drilling in Uganda is most likely to have negative political and environmental impacts, reflecting ongoing public discussion about the country's major oil projects.

Uganda's Tilenga, Kingfisher, and East African Crude Oil Pipeline developments involve drilling in sensitive areas like Murchison Falls National Park and near Lake Albert, with reports of water pollution, dead fish, and habitat disruption for wildlife including elephants.
Documented issues include community displacement, inadequate compensation, activist intimidation, and projected emissions of around 379 million tons of CO2 over 25 years, exceeding current combined annual emissions of Uganda and Tanzania.

The East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) is a 1,443-kilometre electrically heated, buried export line that will carry waxy crude from Uganda’s Albertine Graben oilfields to a marine terminal at Chongoleani, near Tanga on Tanzania’s Indian Ocean coast. As of August–September 2026 it is 91–93% complete, with first oil targeted for late 2026 or January 2027.

Route and design.The line starts at Kabaale in Hoima District (296 km in Uganda) and runs 1,147 km through Tanzania. It is a 24-inch insulated pipe buried about one metre deep, kept at roughly 50°C by electrical heat tracing so the viscous crude does not solidify. Design capacity is 216,000 barrels per day, expandable to 246,000. Infrastructure includes six pump stations, pressure-reduction stations, a 2-million-barrel storage terminal, and a Suezmax loading jetty.
The pipeline will transport commingled crude from two upstream projects: @TotalEnergies -operated Tilenga (peak 190,000 bpd) and CNOOC-operated Kingfisher (40,000 bpd). Uganda has named the export blend “Pearl Sweet.” Recoverable resources in the Lake Albert area are estimated at 1.4–1.7 billion barrels.

Ownership and cost. EACOP Ltd is a special-purpose company owned by TotalEnergies (62%), Uganda National Oil Company (15%), Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (15%), and CNOOC (8%). Construction cost estimates now sit around $5–5.6 billion. Main contractors include China Petroleum Pipeline Engineering and Worley.
Economic case. Uganda and Tanzania present the project as major foreign direct investment, a source of tax and transit revenue, construction jobs, and a new export corridor. Officials argue it will help Uganda convert a 2006 oil discovery into commercial production after years of delay caused by landlocked geography and the need for heating. Project documents also highlight fibre-optic monitoring, some solar power at facilities, and post-construction land restoration.
Climate numbers. The Climate Accountability Institute estimated in 2022 that full-value-chain emissions over a 25-year life—construction, pipeline operation, shipping, refining, and end-use combustion—total about 379 million tonnes of CO₂e. Peak annual emissions were put at roughly 35 million tonnes. The project’s own environmental studies counted only construction and operation emissions, which the institute said represented about 1.8% of the total. EACOP’s later internal figures put its own Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions over 25 years lower (around 5 million tonnes after mitigation measures). Critics treat the pipeline as a mid-sized “carbon bomb”; operators note that Scope 1–2 intensity is comparable to other long-distance lines and that the countries’ national climate plans are not expected to be derailed by the project’s direct emissions.

Environment and land. The route crosses farmland, wetlands, rivers, and areas near the Lake Victoria basin. Well pads and roads have been built inside Murchison Falls National Park for Tilenga. Independent analyses have flagged risks to freshwater systems, wildlife corridors, and seismic zones.

Around Kingfisher, communities and NGOs have reported water-quality complaints, reduced fish catches, and security-force presence. Land acquisition for the pipeline in Uganda affected thousands of households (one official figure is 3,648 project-affected households); broader estimates that include related oil-field works run much higher. Compensation disputes, livelihood loss, and allegations of intimidation of critics have been documented by Climate Rights International, AFIEGO, Just Finance International, and @UN  special rapporteurs. Companies say they follow IFC standards, have resettled people, and are restoring land.

The honest verdict: Uganda is not doomed to an oil curse, and it is already living several of its opening chapters—expectation inflation, fiscal pre-commitment, local dispossession, and governance stress. The curse, if it comes, will not be the geology. It will be treating 2% of GDP as if it were a new country.
I’ll look at Uganda’s succession politics and how control of oil rents, UNOC, and security around the fields could shift as leadership contests intensify.Oil arrives in Uganda at the same moment the political system is shifting from one-man rule toward an unsettled succession. That timing matters more than any single well.

The calendar is the first risk. Museveni won another term in January 2026. First oil is due in late 2026 or early 2027. His son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Defence Forces, has said he will run in 2031 and expects his father’s backing. Other family and party figures, including Odrek Rwabwogo, are treated in Ugandan media as competing centres of influence. There is no formal succession plan. Oil revenues will start while the presidency is still personalised and the next holder of that office is being fought over inside the ruling coalition, not chosen by a settled institutional process.
Oil is a patronage prize before it is a development tool. Uganda’s fiscal rules put almost all spending discretion at the centre. Appointments at UNOC, the Petroleum Authority, the energy ministry, and the security units that guard the Albertine fields and pipeline corridor are the real levers. In a succession contest those posts become loyalty currency: who sits on UNOC’s board, who signs offtake and refinery deals, who controls classified security budgets around Kingfisher and Tilenga. A narrow family-military circle already concentrates coercive power; oil rents can thicken that circle or split it if rival camps try to lock in contracts and jobs before 2031.
The army sits on the resource. Special Forces and other UPDF units protect oil infrastructure. The CDF is both a possible heir and the officer with command over those units. That dual role blurs the line between commercial security and political insurance. If succession stays managed, companies get continuity of protection. If it becomes a faction fight inside the army, the fields and the pipeline become strategic assets to hold, not just industrial sites to operate. Local communities already live with a heavy security presence; a contested transition would likely tighten that presence, not loosen it.
Contracts can look stable and still be politicised. TotalEnergies, CNOOC, and lenders price Uganda on project economics and sovereign risk. They do not vote. They do watch whether a future government reopens production-sharing terms, UNOC’s 15% carried interest, EACOP guarantees, the Vitol loan, or the planned refinery. A successor who needs quick cash or nationalist credentials may push to renegotiate. A successor who needs investor confidence may leave the deals alone. Intra-elite rivalry raises the odds of mixed signals: one camp courting Total and China, another attacking “foreign capture” of Pearl Sweet. That uncertainty is itself a tax on the resource.
Revenue rules will be tested by election-cycle spending. The Petroleum Fund and the cap on oil money in the budget exist on paper. Succession politics rewards visible spending—roads, cash programmes, security payroll—not deposits in a savings reserve. If 2031 is treated as a coronation campaign, expect pressure to pull more oil cash into the Consolidated Fund and UNOC-linked projects that can be branded as the heir’s achievements. The IMF already expects oil to finance new spending rather than close the deficit. A succession race would amplify that.
Western and Chinese partners pull in different directions. Oil ties Uganda more tightly to TotalEnergies (France), CNOOC (China), and Tanzanian transit politics. Muhoozi’s public foreign-policy interventions have already strained some diplomatic channels. A more militarised or family-centred succession could complicate insurance, bank participation, and political-risk cover for EACOP even if the steel is already in the ground. China and commodity traders may care less about democratic form and more about offtake security—so the external constraint on how oil is used may weaken just as domestic contestation rises.
What this means for the resource itself Geology does not change with the presidency. Who captures the rent does. The plausible paths are continuity with tighter military-family control of UNOC and field security; a messy intra-NRM bargain that slows decisions on the refinery, new licences, and Fund withdrawals; or a crisis in which oil sites and pipeline nodes become bargaining chips. None of those paths is required by the constitution. All of them are more likely than a quiet, rules-based handover of a new oil state, because Uganda has not yet had a peaceful transfer of the presidency in the oil era—or in the last forty years.
I’ll pull current assessments of EACOP’s route, spill and climate risks, and the main environmental disputes.EACOP is a 1,443 km buried, electrically heated pipeline from Kabaale, Uganda, to Tanga, Tanzania. It will move waxy Albertine crude that solidifies at ambient temperature, so the line must stay hot for its operating life. Peak throughput is designed around 216,000–246,000 barrels a day. Construction is more than 90% complete; first oil is still targeted for late 2026. The environmental risk is not one issue. It is a stack: water, wildlife, climate, and what happens if the pipe fails.
Water is the highest local risk. Independent spatial analysis finds the route and feeders intersecting 158 wetlands in Uganda, about 230 rivers in some counts, and a long stretch of the Lake Victoria basin—about 460 km of the line sits in that catchment, which supports more than 40 million people. Critical crossings include the Victoria Nile inside Murchison Falls National Park (Tilenga feeder) and the Kibale/Bukoora system that drains toward the SAMUKA Ramsar wetland and Lake Victoria.

The Netherlands Commission for Environmental Assessment called wetland and river crossings the most sensitive construction phase; once they are done, basin-scale damage is hard to reverse.
Open-cut trenching was used on several Ugandan crossings; Tanzania required horizontal directional drilling at Kagera and Sigi after spill modelling showed Lake Victoria at risk. A leak at a river crossing would travel farther and faster than a leak on dry land. Lake Albert fisheries are already a separate concern: produced water and sludge from Kingfisher, plus any slick, would hit a lake that supplies a large share of Uganda’s catch and Congolese livelihoods.
Biodiversity and parks.Tilenga puts well pads and roads inside Murchison Falls National Park—Uganda’s oldest park and last lion stronghold, plus an elephant corridor into South Sudan and DRC. Satellite work has counted on the order of 38 km of roads and nine pads in the park. EACOP and feeders cut a chimpanzee corridor between Wambabya and Bugoma forests. Habitat-overlap figures cited in 2026 reporting: about 84% of the route with antelope range, 67% monkey, 22% leopard, 17% giraffe. At Tanga, mangrove clearance for the terminal and jetty has been documented; those stands are high-value carbon and fishery habitat. The Great Rift is seismically active; a 2016 quake near the route damaged buildings. A heated, pressurized line across rift ground raises spill probability over 25 years even if daily leak rates are low.
Climate.Burning the oil EACOP is built to carry is estimated at about 379 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent over 25 years—on the order of 34 million tonnes a year, more than Uganda and Tanzania emit together today, and roughly 40 years of Uganda’s current domestic emissions. That is a global-atmosphere risk, not a local spill risk. It is why dozens of banks and insurers declined project finance.
What the companies say they are doing. EACOP reports land reinstatement, tree planting (130,000-plus trees cited), work with the National Forestry Authority at Taala Forest, and a planned offset in the Rwizi watershed for grey crowned crane habitat. A Tanga coastal restoration programme is pledged; advisers say mangrove, seagrass and coral recovery can take 20–30 years. Lender due-diligence papers have described the project as broadly aligned with IFC standards, with an outstanding biodiversity action tied to CNOOC’s Kingfisher facilities. Those measures reduce, they do not remove, residual risk
The pipeline is now in its final construction and commissioning phase. Whether first oil proceeds on the current timetable, and whether remaining legal and community disputes alter operations, will be the next test of a project that has been planned for more than a decade.
The EACOP carbon numbers look contradictory until you separate what is being counted. One set measures the pipeline’s own energy use. The other measures the oil the pipeline will move once it is burned.

Company and lender figures (Scope 1 and 2)
EACOP’s later operational estimate is 5.05 million tonnes of CO₂e over 25 years, down from an original base case of 8.88 Mt after shifting most power from crude-fired generators to national grids plus batteries and some solar. Construction Scope 1+2 is on the order of 0.45–0.5 Mt. TotalEnergies reports Tilenga plus EACOP at about 13 kg CO₂e per barrel for Scopes 1 and 2, versus a company average near 18–19 kg and a higher African-project average. Combined Tilenga + EACOP Scope 1+2 over 25 years is cited at roughly 13.5 Mt; Tilenga life-of-field Scope 1+2 was later put at 12.85 Mt. Peak annual Scope 1+2 for Tilenga and EACOP together is given as about 0.8 Mt.

Average about 15 Mt/year; peak plateau about 34.8 Mt/year. Construction plus pipeline operation is only 1.8% of that total. CAI used 390 kg CO₂ per barrel for product use after subtracting non-energy uses (8%). Peak annual full-chain emissions would exceed Uganda and Tanzania’s combined fossil-fuel emissions at the time of the study.

How to read the gap
The 5 Mt and 379 Mt figures are not rival measurements of the same thing. The first is midstream energy use. The second is the carbon in the crude the line is built to export. If the oil is produced and sold, most of those 331 Mt of combustion emissions happen regardless of who reports them. If the oil stays in the ground, they do not. That is why critics call EACOP a “carbon bomb” and why operators emphasize intensity per barrel and grid-powered pumps.
Limits of both datasets
CAI excluded upstream field emissions (Tilenga/Kingfisher flaring, power, drilling), so the true project-system total is higher than 379 Mt. Company figures exclude most Scope 3 by design. Throughput could rise if other fields (including possible DRC volumes) use the line. ESIA operational numbers that CAI used were incomplete and have since been revised downward by EACOP’s grid-power plan. Intensity claims depend on allocation between pipeline and fields and on whose barrels are in the denominator.
Practical comparison
At 216,000 bpd plateau, full-chain emissions of ~35 Mt/year are large relative to the two host countries’ fossil inventories and small relative to global oil combustion. Direct pipeline operations of a few hundred thousand tonnes a year are modest for a 1,443 km heated line. The climate significance of EACOP is almost entirely the oil it enables, not the electricity that keeps the wax flowing.
I'll look up Uganda's oil-revenue laws, EITI status, published numbers, and recent audits so the analysis is current.Uganda has built a formal oil-revenue system on paper. The real test begins when commercial production starts later in 2026 or 2027. So far, most “oil money” is still fees and taxes from exploration and development, not profit oil.
The legal pipeline

The Public Finance Management Act (2015) requires petroleum revenues to enter a dedicated Petroleum Fund first. From there they can move to the Consolidated Fund for the budget, a Petroleum Revenue Investment Reserve (PRIR) for future generations, or—after a 2021 amendment—to the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC). Withdrawals need parliamentary appropriation and Auditor General involvement. Spending from oil receipts is supposed to go to infrastructure and development, not routine consumption. The finance minister must table inflow/outflow estimates and semi-annual and annual Fund reports in Parliament and publish them.
A fiscal rule allows only a capped share of non-oil GDP (about 0.8% of the previous year’s non-oil GDP) into the annual budget; the rest is meant for savings. That rule has not yet been stress-tested by large production revenues. The PRIR investment framework has also lagged.

What the books show today
As of 30 June 2025 the Petroleum Fund held Shs 131.27 billion, down from Shs 145.98 billion a year earlier. In FY 2024/25 government transferred Shs 115.4 billion to the Consolidated Fund and Shs 166.5 billion to UNOC. Sources were still pre-production: company taxes, surface rentals, data sales, training and licensing fees, signature bonuses. Oil-and-gas related collections reported in sector monitoring were about Shs 208 billion in FY 2024/25. The FY 2026/27 budget assumes Shs 1.44 trillion in petroleum revenue—still a small slice of an Shs 84 trillion national budget. Officials project a government share of 65–80% of upstream revenues at peak. Independent estimates of eventual annual take often sit around $1.5–2.5 billion, highly sensitive to price and cost recovery.
UNOC itself is becoming a large fiscal actor. It posted a large profit in FY 2024/25 from a government-backed fuel-import arrangement with Vitol, received Fund transfers for operations, and won parliamentary approval for a large Vitol-linked loan. That mix—commercial trading, equity in Tilenga/Kingfisher/EACOP, and Fund financing—makes UNOC disclosure as important as Fund disclosure.
EITI and public reporting
Uganda joined the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative in 2020. Its first validation scored 78.5/100 (moderate progress). EITI reports reconcile company payments with government receipts, but they have covered a pre-production sector and have shown reconciliation gaps (one report noted gaps up to 53%), thin sub-national transfer data, and incomplete contract and beneficial-ownership disclosure. A second validation is scheduled for 1 October 2026—just as first oil is expected. That timing matters: the next reports will have to cover profit oil, cost recovery, and midstream tariffs, not only fees.
Where transparency is still thin
Researchers at the Natural Resource Governance Institute and local groups such as ACODE flag several gaps that the law does not fully close:
Contracts and costs. Production-sharing terms, recoverable costs, and some midstream agreements are not fully public. Cost recovery will determine how much “profit oil” actually reaches the Fund in the early years.
What counts as petroleum revenue. It is not fully settled in law whether EACOP tariffs, refinery income, and all UNOC dividends must pass through the Fund.
UNOC’s dual role. Transfers from the Fund to the national oil company, plus UNOC’s ability to retain trading profits, can pull money off the standard appropriation path unless Parliament gets investment plans and scenario forecasts in advance.
Spending verification. There is still no strong public mechanism to confirm that money taken from the Fund for “infrastructure and development” was spent that way.
Sub-national share. Statute exists; actual published transfers remain limited.
The @IMFNews  has separately stressed stronger anti-corruption and governance institutions as production starts. Government officials, including Finance Minister Henry Musasizi, say statements are audited and “guardrails” are in place. That claim is checkable: Fund reports, Auditor General opinions on UNOC, EITI reconciliations, and published production volumes and prices after first oil.

What to watch after first crude
Transparency will be judged less by the existence of a Petroleum Fund than by a short list of numbers: barrels produced, price realized for “Pearl Sweet,” cost-oil versus profit-oil split, government receipts by instrument, transfers to the budget versus UNOC versus the savings reserve, and whether those figures match company filings. Until those line up in public, Uganda has a revenue architecture. It does not yet have a production-era transparency record.
Uganda’s oil-revenue system is detailed on paper and still lightly tested in practice. Commercial production has not started; almost all money in the Petroleum Fund so far is pre-production tax and fees, not profit oil from Tilenga, Kingfisher, or EACOP.
How the money is supposed to move
The Public Finance Management Act (2015) requires petroleum receipts to enter a Petroleum Fund first. From there they can go to the Consolidated Fund (budget), a Petroleum Revenue Investment Reserve for future generations, or—after a 2021 amendment—to the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC). Withdrawals need parliamentary appropriation. Oil money is meant for infrastructure and development, not routine spending. A fiscal rule caps how much can enter the annual budget (about 0.8% of the previous year’s non-oil GDP).

According to remand copy, Rohan Parekh had been posing as an official from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO). 

A fake digital ID card of PMO was recovered from his possession.

The police have registered a case under sections 204, 205, 3(5), 319(2), 335, 336, 337, and 340 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).

Another accused in the case, Prathamesh Bagul, is currently absconding, and a search for him is underway.

Rohan Parekh's lawyer claimed in court that an individual named Tarun Gupta had allegedly entrapped Rohan using a fake PMO email. 

According to the lawyer, Rohan had received a job offer to work at the PMO. 

Subsequently, he was provided with the alleged PMO digital ID card and a letter of appreciation purportedly bearing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's signature.

The lawyer stated that Rohan had studied in London and was working on subjects related to geopolitics and defense policy. 

The letter of appreciation claimed to commend his work at the United Nations (UN) and his writings on geopolitics. 

The lawyer maintains that these documents are forged and that Rohan himself is a victim of this alleged fraud.

In court, the lawyer also claimed that Rohan had arrived at NMACC about 24 hours before the Prime Minister's event, stating that he had gone there solely to purchase perfume. 

He told the police that he had no connection to the Prime Minister's event.

Rohan was accompanied by his bodyguard, Dilip Kunde.

Kunde is reported to be a former Army personnel. A weapon has been recovered from him.

Investigation will now aim at determining who created the fake PMO ID and documents, what role Tarun Gupta played, and the identity of the person who offered Rohan a job at the PMO.
A search is also underway for the absconding accused, Prathamesh Bagul.

text:
Tragic Philosophical Dialogue

South of Antioch, Syria, Eastern Roman Empire

October 28th, 637 A.D.
--------------------------------------------------------

The sea beats a heavy, measured rhythm against the cliffs below, a restless percussion drifting through the single iron-barred window of the arched stone cell. With it comes the sharp, salt-laden wind and the sudden, wheeling cries of gulls catching the thermals above the East Mediterranean coast.

Inside, the light is gray and angled, cutting through the salt-crusted bars to illuminate the damp flagstones worn down by age and usage.

Tariq stands near the center of the vault. He wears a tunic of fine, dyed wool in a deep indigo, belted with tooled leather, and a mantle of pale Syrian linen draped cleanly over his shoulder. The hem of his garment is free of the red dust outside, clean-pressed and dignified-the attire of a man who walks with the authority of the new administration, yet remembers the humble fabric of his beginnings.

Before him, chained to a low iron ring driven deep into the rear wall, the captive sits upon the bare stone. Stripped of his heavy vestments, the middle aged cleric wears only a coarse linen loincloth, his skin pale and marked by the sudden chill of the coastal draft. Yet, as he lifts his head, his gaze holds a steady, unyielding clarity that the iron cuffs cannot diminish.

"You bring the smell of cloves and fresh bread into a tomb, scholar," the cleric says, his voice raspy from disuse, carrying the cadence of Greek liturgy. "Tell me, does the commander of the garrison send you to debate the nature of the Trinity, or merely to inspect the quality of his chains once more?"

Tariq steps closer, his soft-soled boots clicking against the damp floor. He folds his hands within his sleeves, looking down not with cruelty, but with the quiet scrutiny of a man examining an ancient manuscript found in a sacked library.

"Neither," Tariq replies, his Arabic clear and deliberate, though touched by the local Aramaic phrasing. "The garrison commander cares only for ransoms and troop movements. I came because the guards said you spent the night reciting the Psalms of David in the dark while the surf hammered the rocks. A man who sings when he is starving usually has a destination in his mind. I wanted to know where you thought you were going whilst trapped in this cell. I'm curios."

The captive shifts, the iron chain rattling sharply against the stone. He pulls his knees closer to his chest to ward off the chill.

"Curiosity is natural, yet I go to the same place you are, Imam, whether you call it the Kingdom or the final judgment," the cleric answers, his eyes tracking the dust motes dancing in the bar of sunlight. "Though I suspect your path involves fewer iron rings. You come dressed like a magistrate of Antioch, yet you stand in a dungeon. Which of us is truly bound by lies, the city has yet to fall."

Tariq smiles faintly, stepping toward the barred window to look out at the white-capped expanse of the sea stretching toward Cyprus.

"Yet, to fall...precisely. You speak of freedom as if it were a mood, monk. But the world has shifted beneath your feet while you chanted in your scriptorium. The old banners have fallen, not because God abandoned them, but because their time ran out like sand in an hourglass. We do not come to erase the prophets, but to complete the ledger they left behind unfinished by first the Jews and now you, Christians."

"You come with the sword not logic," the captive says softly, leaning his head back against the cold stone wall. "And when you attempt to come with logic you, instead, come with a book dictated to a merchant in the desert, as if the whispers of angels could unseat the councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon. You ask me where I am going? I am sitting in the wreckage of a world that understood the mystery of God, while you build tents on its ruins and call them an empire."

Tariq turns slowly from the window, the sea wind fluttering the edge of his linen mantle. He looks down at the chained man, his expression hardening into one of absolute conviction.

"An empire? No. Empires are built on taxes and blood, and they crumble when the wine turns sour," Tariq says, his voice dropping an octave, resonating within the vaulted stone. "We built a submission. Not to men, not to councils of bishops arguing over Greek syllables, but to the One who made both the sea outside and the salt in your throat. You call it wreckage. We call it the clearing of the ground so the foundation could finally be laid straight."

"You speak with confidence, yet the knowledge spoken, is like that of a child. Why cannot you see, Tariq, that Submission is not built-it is demanded, or given. Willingly, or unwillingly. Why turn from the Lord God, to serve these people who displace our kindred? What have you gained, Scholar?"

The cleric’s words strike with the dry, biting crispness of desert salt, stripping away the polished veneer of the debate. Tariq does not flinch, nor does he step back. For a long moment, the only sound in the arched cell is the steady, indifferent crash of the Mediterranean surf against the stone cliffs outside and the sharp rattle of the captive’s iron chain as he shifts his weight.

Tariq unfolds his hands from his sleeves, his gaze locking onto the priest’s bloodshot eyes. The refined composure of the magistrate’s scholar remains, but beneath it, the quiet memory of a world before the banners changed flickers to life.

"You speak of demands, monk, as if man ever needed a revelation to learn how to demand things at the point of a spear," Tariq says, his voice low and steady, lacking its previous oratorical flourish. "Every king in Antioch, every Caesar in Constantinople, every prefect who ever collected a grain tax built his throne on compulsion. They demanded obedience with legions and tax collectors, and when the walls cracked, they wept because their forced masonry could not hold."

He takes a slow step forward, looking down at the bare stone floor between them, then back up to the captive.

"You ask what I have gained," Tariq continues, the bitter cadence of the real world edging into his tone. "Do you think I was born in this cloak of dyed wool? My people tended the dry hills south of here while your bishops drank from golden chalices they taxed from olive farmers. We watched the armies of Heraclius march past our doors, bleeding us dry to pay for wars against the Persians-wars that left both empires hollow shells, fit only to be knocked over like rotten timber."

Tariq gestures vaguely toward the barred window, where the vast, salt-scented air moves across the coast.

"I did not turn from the Lord God. I stopped serving the intermediaries who made His name a brand for imperial tax policy. Submission is not given willingly to an army, and it cannot be sustained forever by the lash. But when a people bow not to a Caesar, not to a patriarch, but to an absolute law that binds the king and the slave alike... that is not a displacement of kindred. That is an end to the cycle."

The Imam lets out a slow breath, his fingers resting lightly on the leather belt at his waist.

"You sit there in chains, lamenting the displacement of your kindred, while the men who wore your robes spent centuries bickering over whether Christ had one will or two while the poor starved in the alleys," Tariq says quietly. "I have gained a world that finally makes sense. Have you?"

"I hear clearly what YOU have gained. YOU have gained much from this, as OTHERS, are suffering. You, are like Judas. You changed from one master, to another for your own benefit. YOU, again, gained. Yet what of the children now?

 The boys who have not matured, have been taken, the boys who were mature-are dead. The men of fighting age, are dead. Every female child from freshly born to before puberty, have been stolen, those past puberty, violated and separated from their mothers, made into secondary wives-if you can call it that-at night you can hear them screaming, crying-then silence. 

The next morning, their body being removed from the home...their use to the invader, over. Their insolence a reason to kill them, after violating them. They are like cattle now...something...something you should remember from your time in the hills, Scholar..."

The cleric’s voice drops from theological debate into a heavy, suffocating quiet, stripped of all pretense and academic polish. The grand arguments of empires and creeds dissolve against the brutal, immediate horror of the street outside-the raw, inescapable cost of conquest that no treaty or theology can sanitize.

Tariq flinches. It is not a dramatic recoil, but a sudden, rigid stiffening of his frame, as if a physical blow has landed just beneath his ribs. The confident posture of the magistrate’s scholar vanishes, leaving only the man who remembers the smell of dust and woodsmoke in the southern hills. He looks down at the stone floor, his jaw tightening so hard the muscles shift beneath his skin. The rhythmic crash of the Mediterranean surf outside suddenly feels deafening, a indifferent pulse mocking the fragility of human rationalization.

"You think I do not hear it?" Tariq speaks, his voice cracking slightly, losing its measured cadence. He does not shout; the words come out flat, forced through a throat tight with a sudden, suffocating disgust. "You think because I wear a clean tunic and walk the paved streets of Antioch that the noise of the night does not reach my ears? You think I traded masters to sleep soundly while the ditches fill?"

He takes a sharp, uneven step toward the wall, his hands clenching into fists within the folds of his indigo sleeves. The memory of the hills-the harsh, honest survival of tending sheep among the rocks-flashes behind his eyes, juxtaposed against the grim realities of war that the victors prefer to drape in pious rhetoric.

"Do not speak to me of Judas," Tariq whispers, his gaze lifting to meet the captive’s eyes, revealing a raw, tormented depth that the chains cannot cage. "Judas sold a man for silver. What happened out there-what happens when any banner falls and the wolves are let loose-is older than the Gospels, older than the Torah. It is the blood-tax of the spear. Every army that ever marched under a cross, an eagle, or a crescent has left that exact trail of ash and broken flesh behind it."

He turns away, running a hand over his face, his breath coming short and heavy.

"You call them cattle. You ask what I have gained," Tariq says, his voice dropping to a harsh rasp as he stares out the narrow barred window at the indifferent blue of the sea. "I gained a law that forbids it. I gained a book that curses the men who do it to the lowest pits of the Fire. But laws do not instantly cleanse the blood from a soldier's hands, and ink on parchment cannot raise the dead children in the alleyways."

He turns back to face the cleric, his eyes burning with a desperate, defensive fury.

"The men who did those things tonight-who broke oaths and dragged innocents from their beds-they wear our turbans now, just as your countrymen wore the purple when they burned the villages of the borderlands. Do you think God looks at the color of their cloaks and calls it righteousness? They will answer for every scream in that darkness, monk. Every last one of them. And so will I, if I stood by and called it the will of heaven."

"Your conscience and prior history...betray you scholar. You cannot combine the word and laws of Christ and your new 'faith'. Is it not written in your new book, that women in conquered lands, are spoils of war? Are not the infidel, the Jew and the Christian, to be eliminated-hunted even? I fear you walk a path that leads to darkness, forcing a torch into your hands. Instead of a path of light, where no torch is needed, Scholar."

The cleric’s words settle over the damp stone floor like frost, heavy and unsparing, cutting past every defense the scholar has tried to build. For a long moment, Tariq does not move. The confident scholar of the new administration is gone, leaving only a man standing rigidly in the gray light of the barred window, the salt breeze carrying the distant, mocking cry of the gulls.

"You speak of a path without a torch," Tariq says, his voice barely above a whisper, rough with a sudden, bitter sorrow. "Yet the world you defend was lit entirely by the fires of burning villages, fueled by emperors who traded in blood and bishops who burned their neighbors over Greek vowels. You call my faith darkness because it does not offer the comfort of an old illusion."

He steps closer, his gaze falling upon the chained man not with anger, but with a profound, aching weariness.

"You ask if the book commands the hunting of the infidel, the subjugation of the weak," Tariq continues, his shoulders sinking as the weight of the age presses down upon him. "It commands justice. It commands mercy when the sword is sheathed. But men-men with iron in their fists and lust in their hearts-take the sacred text and twist it into a license for their own cruelty, just as your kings used the cross to justify the slaughter of anyone who did not bow to Constantinople."

He reaches out, his fingers brushing the cold iron bars of the cell window, looking out toward the horizon where the sea meets the sky in an unyielding line.

"Perhaps you are right, monk. Perhaps we have only traded one set of executioners for another, wrapping our ancient sins in new banners," Tariq murmurs, closing his eyes against the glaring light. "You hold the chains, and I hold the keys. But if this path is darkness, it is the only one left where the sun might eventually rise. Your old world is dead, priest. And neither of our prayers will bring it back."

"You speak of men-Emperors and beyond who I have no sway, nor you, over. I speak of what is outside these walls. The voices, the cries...then the silence. The world, here, is gone as I know it-yes. Yet the Lord God, is not. And as long as the word of the Lord God is spoken on my lips, shall He forever be in this world. For I am His beloved son, for I do good in His-"

The sharp crack of flesh against flesh echoes off the damp stone walls, swallowing the cleric’s final words mid-sentence.

Tariq’s hand remains suspended in the air for a fraction of a second, trembling slightly before he slowly pulls it back and presses it flat against the coarse fabric of his indigo sleeve. The measured, academic scholar is entirely shattered; in his place stands a man raw with a terrifying, defensive panic. His chest heaves beneath the fine wool, and his eyes are wide, glittering with a mixture of fury and sudden, desperate grief.

The captive’s head has snapped sideways from the force of the blow. A dark line of blood wells instantly from the corner of his split lip, trickling down over his pale, stubbled jaw to drip onto his bare chest. Yet, he does not flinch away or cower. Slowly, agonizingly, he turns his head back, his swollen lips parting in a grim, defiant smile. He fixes his reddened, unwavering gaze straight into Tariq’s eyes.

"You struck me," the cleric whispers, his voice tasting of iron, yet dripping with a quiet, vindictive triumph. "You struck a man in chains who spoke of the living God. Tell me, Scholar... which scripture taught you that terror is the answer to the truth?"

Tariq steps back, his boots scraping sharply against the flagstones, fleeing an inch from the prisoner as if the man’s very presence is catching fire. He runs a trembling hand over his face, pressing his fingers hard against his eyes, his breathing ragged and shallow. The illusion of authority, the carefully constructed armor of the new administration, lies broken at their feet.

"You think this is courage?" Tariq snarls, his voice dropping into a venomous, vibrating hiss that fills the vaulted stone cell far more effectively than any shout.

Tariq drops down onto one knee right before the chained cleric, ignoring the filth and the chill of the stones. He reaches out, his hand gripping the rough linen of the prisoner’s ragged clothing at the collarbone, hauling him forward so the heavy iron cuffs rattle viciously against the wall.

"You sit in the dark, wrapped in your martyr's pride, daring the world to break you because it costs you nothing!" Tariq’s face is inches from the cleric’s, his eyes burning with a wild, unrestrained rage, the fine wool of his indigo tunic straining across his chest. "You invoke a God of mercy while you weaponize the suffering of innocents just to score theological points against a man who actually has to walk among the ruins you lament!"

The cleric’s bloody lip parts in a tight, mocking smirk, his eyes glinting with stubborn defiance. "Then do it," the priest whispers, tasting his own blood. "Strike me again, Imam. Show me how your new law heals the world my Christ gave His life for. Show me how you, an earthly whore of literature, can supercede my Lord God. The Christ"

Tariq’s breath hitches, his fingers tightening so hard his knuckles turn white against the fabric. Every muscle in his arm trembles, not with fear, but with the brutal, violent urge to shatter the smug, untouchable certainty in the captive’s gaze. For a fraction of a second, the abyss opens between them-the raw impulse of the conqueror meeting the unyielding stubbornness of the conquered.

With a guttural exhalation of pure disgust, Tariq violently shoves the cleric back against the stone wall. The chains clatter wildly, echoing off the arched ceiling as the prisoner’s head hits the masonry with a dull thud.

Tariq rises to his feet, smoothing the front of his linen mantle with a violent, trembling jerk. He does not look down as he turns his back on the bleeding man.

"Keep your God, monk," Tariq says, his voice cold, flat, and absolute, cutting through the sound of the surf like a knife. "And keep your prayers. But know this-when the sun rises over Antioch tomorrow, the men who built this world will still be awake, trying to keep it from drowning in the blood your precious emperors left behind. You are nothing more than a ghost rattling your chains in an empty room."

He slams his palm against the heavy timber door once more, hard enough to rattle the iron bolts. Without waiting for the guards to finish drawing the heavy bars, he stands shrouded in the shadows, waiting for the wood to open so he can step back into the storm.

"Better I were a ghost blessed with the knowledge of Christ...for you are a fool wrapped in the linen, others have given you-with a pat on the head, like a dog"

The insult lands with the cold precision of a dropped blade.

Tariq’s hand, resting against the heavy timber of the door, freezes. The remaining heat in his chest instantly hardens into something brittle and razor-sharp. He does not turn around immediately; he stands motionless in the gray shaft of light, listening to the heavy, uneven breathing of the man bound to the floor and the distant, rhythmic crash of the surf beyond the bars.

Slowly, Tariq turns his head over his shoulder, his dark eyes narrowing into a dangerous, glacial squint. The fury has burned down to a white-hot coal, leaving his voice eerily quiet as it cuts through the damp air.

"A dog," Tariq repeats softly, the word tasting like ash on his tongue. "You think I wear this linen because I begged for scraps at a conqueror’s table?"

He takes two measured steps back into the center of the cell, looking down at the cleric not with the heat of a brawl, but with the cold disdain of a man staring down an insect.

"You imagine that because the banners changed, the men holding the pikes are all strangers from some mythical desert," Tariq says, his voice dropping into a low, vibrating register. "Look at my hands, monk. Look at the calluses. I dug the ditches of this province before the first horseman crossed the border. I buried my cousins in the rocky soil of the southern hills while your prefects in Antioch sat drinking watered wine and debating whether Christ possessed two wills or one."

He steps closer, towering over the seated prisoner, his shadow swallowing the pale light on the floor.

"I did not take a master's pat on the head," Tariq snarls, the control finally cracking to reveal the raw, wounded pride beneath. "I took a seat at the table because the old masters left nothing behind but empty storehouses and bleeding children. If that makes me a dog in your eyes, then at least I am guarding a house that stands, while you sit in the dark, chained to the skeleton of a palace that deserved to fall."

"You forget every teaching the Lord God gave us...you trade again what YOU have done, what YOU deemed worthy, what caused YOU strife to be worthy of your position now. It means nothing. You, like I have said, are a dog. A useful pawn. 

Hmph, you think you are going to walk into Antioch with them, hm? As a Greek-Aramaic convert? You will be given the least of the lands, for in the book, only the Arabs are most worthy of praise, property and respect. Over time you'll find yourself relegated, contested, and removed...just like the other fools before you"

The cleric’s words strike with the dry, prophetic finality of an ancient tomb sealing shut. They cut past the anger, past the defense of the ditches and the dead cousins, hitting upon the cold, gnawing anxiety that Tariq has buried beneath layers of fine wool and administrative ledgers.

Tariq goes entirely still. The fire drains from his posture, leaving him standing rigid in the dim, salt-heavy air of the cell. He looks down at the bleeding, broken man before him, and for a terrifying second, the reflection of his own future stares back from the cleric’s eyes-a realization of the outsider who believed himself an architect, only to find himself a disposable tool.

"And what of it?" Tariq asks, his voice dropping into a harsh, hollow whisper that barely carries over the relentless percussion of the sea outside.

He does not deny it. He does not shout, nor does he strike the prisoner again. Instead, he lets the bitter truth hang heavily between them in the gray dust motes.

"You think I haven't watched them? You think I don't see the way the tribal chieftains from the Hejaz look at us-at men who speak Arabic with the rough, broken accent of the northern borderlands, who smell of olive oil and church stone instead of camel dust and palm dates?" Tariq’s shoulders sink, the heavy mantle of his pride suddenly feeling impossibly burdensome. "They look at our conversions as tribute. They look at our learning as a tool to be used and then discarded when the administration is running."

He turns his gaze slowly toward the barred window, watching a single gull wheel against the pale sky above the Mediterranean breakers.

"Yes, they write their preferences into the laws. Yes, the blood of the desert claims the first seats at the feast," Tariq murmurs, his tone flat, devoid of its former defense, steeped in the lonely realization of the apostate and the turncoat. "They will take our taxes, they will use our scribes, and when the borders are secure, they will push us to the margins. We will be too Arab for the Greeks, and too Greek for the Arabs-strangers in the only homes we have left."

Tariq turns back to the cleric, his expression worn down to a grim, exhausted resolve.

"You call me a pawn, monk. Perhaps I am. Perhaps I am building the stairs for men who will kick me down the moment I reach the top," Tariq says quietly, taking a slow step back toward the heavy wooden door. "But at least the stairs are being built. At least something out of this ash is rising, even if I am only meant to be buried beneath its foundation."

The cleric’s voice ceases, leaving only the relentless, heavy wash of the Mediterranean tide echoing against the stone foundations below. The warning hangs in the damp air like sea mist, cold and inescapable, refusing to offer comfort or closure.

Tariq stands motionless in the center of the cell, the gray light cutting through the iron bars to catch the fine weave of his indigo tunic. He does not turn back to hurl another denial, nor does he raise a hand to strike the prisoner again. The fury has burned itself out, leaving behind the stark, hollow silence of a man standing entirely alone in a room he helped construct.

He looks down at the blood staining the flagstones near the iron ring-a small, dark pool from the cleric's split lip-and then slowly raises his eyes to the barred window. Outside, the tide continues its ancient, unyielding advance, clawing at the cliffs, indifferent to the empires that rise and fall upon its shores.

"The tide comes for both our houses, monk," Tariq says quietly

"No,...I walk TO Christ with my suffering. You walk away from Him with your betrayal. I have turned to Righteousness-you? You have turned to what He opposes most in His Heart. Be gone from me."

You can ignore facts and nature all you want, and wish that the world would see your kindness, but a snake is still a snake, a wild animial is still a wild animal. 

Timothy Treadwell spent 13 summers living unprotected among wild coastal brown bears in Katmai National Park, believing he had built a unique bond of mutual trust with the animals. In October 2003, Treadwell and his girlfriend, Amie Huguenard, remained in the park late into the season when food became scarce. A 28-year-old male grizzly attacked Treadwell outside his tent and killed Huguenard when she attempted to defend him, leaving behind a tragic audio recording that captured the fatal encounter.

Kelly Ann Walz raised a black bear named Teddy from a cub on her Pennsylvania property, caring for the animal over a nine-year period alongside other exotic wildlife. In 2009, she entered the bear's enclosure with a shovel of dog food intended to distract the 350-pound animal while she cleaned the cage. The bear unexpectedly turned on her before eating, mauling her to death in front of witnesses before a neighbor shot the animal to retrieve her body.

Stephan Miller was an experienced exotic animal handler who helped raise and train Rocky, a 700-pound grizzly bear famous for appearing in the movie Semi-Pro. During a 2008 promotional video shoot at a California training facility, Miller performed a routine bear-wrestling maneuver he had practiced countless times before. Without warning, Rocky bit Miller directly in the neck, inflicting a single fatal wound before other handlers could intervene with pepper spray.

Donna Munson spent decades illegally feeding wild black bears on her rural Colorado property, treating the local bear population as gentle neighborhood pets despite persistent warnings from state wildlife officials. In July 2009, a large, aggressive male bear arrived at her deck demanding food. When the 80-year-old woman stepped outside to offer a meal, the animal attacked and killed her on her doorstep before wildlife officers arrived and euthanized the bear.

text:
🔸 September 8 - The Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos 🔸

Today we commemorate the Great Feast of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos. The blessed Virgin Mary was born in the small city of Galilee, Nazareth. Her father the Righteous Joachim was of the tribe of King David, and her mother Anna was from the tribe of the First Priest Aaron. The couple was without a child and old in age, but they did not lose faith in God’s mercy, and maintained their hope that He would be able to overcome their barrenness.

They vowed to dedicate the child which the Lord might give them to His service in the Temple. Childlessness was considered a divine punishment for sin among the Hebrews, so Joachim and Anna were slandered by their own countrymen. On one of the feastdays at the Temple in Jerusalem, Joachim brought his sacrifice to offer to God, but the High Priest would not accept it, considering him to be unworthy since he was childless.

In deep grief, St Joachim retreated into the wilderness, and there he prayed with tears entreating the Lord for a child. When St Anna learned what had happened at the Temple, she also wept bitterly in her own garden, not complaining to God, but rather praying for His mercy. In that moment, the Archangel Gabriel appeared to them separately, and announced the joyous news that St Anna would conceive and bear a daughter named Mary, who would be blessed and become a mother to the Savior of the world.

On the right of the first icon, St Joachim receives the revelation from the Archangel Gabriel that he would bear the most blessed daughter. In the top left, he and St Anna share an embrace having received this joyous news. St Anna is shown reclining on her bed as she contemplates this miraculous birth. She gazes at the infant Theotokos who is wrapped in swaddling bands in a cradle. 

They are attended to by midwives who have prepared a feast for this joyous event. The Nativity of the Theotokos marks a dawn of salvation, for in her birth the way is prepared for Christ’s coming. Where Eve brought disobedience, the purity of the Mother of God made possible the Incarnation, through which the Fall is reversed and mankind is redeemed.

text:
A Roman Temple Service layout
(with animal, but without slaughter)

Temple set up:
The room is sparse, except for a dais at the far end in which the deity’s icon stands. The dais itself is surrounded by a curtain which is drawn closed at the beginning of the rite concealing the deity.  In the center of the temple space is a double cubed shaped altar mimicking the fire altars of Ancient Rome, but it is portable with handles on two of its sides. This altar hold the blessed oil lamp/s, blessed lustral waters, and a turibulum(incense burner) and an acerra(container of resin).
Offering items such as wine, and food items are placed around this portable altar. There is also a small amount of feed present to be offered to the sacred animal.
The animal sacred to the deity is held safely outside the temple space or in an adjacent room and is dressed in ribbons, bells, and wreaths, in a way that is safe for the animal.

Pompa(Procession):
The people file into the temple and stand on the sides leaving space open around the central altar, followed by the flamen(priest leading the ritual, and the other sacredotes(fellow priests). The flamen stands right behind the central altar and another sacredos, holding the prayers which the flamen will read, stands next to him.

Praefatio(opening prayer):
The flamen places one piece of resin onto the turibulum and says a prayer to Janus asking for him to open and bless the rite itself.
The flamen then holds aloft the oil lamp and recites the prayer to Hestia for the same. He lights the lamp.

Precatio Prima(first prayer to deity)
This established the point of the ceremony/festival.
The priest recites the opening prayer to the god celebrated, including some epithets, the offerings being made, and why.

Immolatio(consecration of the animal)
The flamen asks for silence, then signals to a sacerdos to being the animal in. The animal is brought to the altar where the priest recites a small prayer, and sprinkles the blessed water and wine on its head, then blessed flour on its back. The sacredos then leads the animal in a procession around the temple space, stopping in front of the curtained dais. The flamen greets the animal with a small amount of food appropriate for the animal and feeds it. The sacerdos who is handling the animal then leads the animal back out of the temple space, and the flamen returns back to the altar.

Invocatio: 
Here the flamen recites the longer prayer to the deity, asking for its presence, using most if not all of the epithets, in increasing power, volume and intensity. At the climax of the invocation, another sacredos sounds a horn, the curtain around the dais is thrown open to reveal the icon, and the drummers & other musicians start playing the music. 

Redditio:
Sacredotes then pick up the offerings and altar in the center of the temple space, and move them aside. The flamen climbs up the steps and joins the deity icon on the dais, and the attending crowd is allowed to fill the central temple space to better view the deity and flamen. One by one the sacredotes hand the offerings to the flamen who then offers it to the icon in several passes, starting with food items, then liquids, then incense, and finally the oil lamp itself. The congregation of worshipers are encouraged to sing and dance as they watch.

Benedictio epularum(blessing of the feast):
The sacredotes bring in a small portion of the banquet feast on a platter to the dais, and the flamen then places one of the food offerings given to deity onto the platter blessing the food underneath. This platter of food is then returned by the sacredotes to join the rest of the food of the banquet, blessing the whole of the banquet. Worshipers are allowed to either join the banquet or stay and continue praising the deity.

Epilogus(closing):
After the incense is completely out, the flamen may bow to the icon, give kiss sign, and descend the dais, while the curtains are again drawn to conceal the deity. Final blessing to deity.

text:
You're making a fundamental mistake: you're taking every occurrence of the English word “one” and pretending it must carry exactly the same meaning regardless of context.

Genesis 2:24 says a husband and wife become “one flesh.” It literally tells you the category of unity being discussed: flesh. Nobody argues that every biblical use of “one” therefore means two separate persons united relationally.

Now read what God says about HIMSELF:

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is ONE LORD.” — Deuteronomy 6:4

“Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.” — Isaiah 43:10

“Beside me there is no God.” — Isaiah 44:6

“I am the LORD... that stretcheth forth the heavens ALONE; that spreadeth abroad the earth BY MYSELF.” — Isaiah 44:24

That's not merely “two divine beings who cooperate perfectly.” God explicitly denies another God beside Him.

And John 17 doesn't overturn that. Jesus praying that believers “may be one, as we are” describes the unity He desires among believers. It doesn't redefine the nature of God or suddenly turn Deuteronomy 6:4 into “multiple divine beings united as one.” You're taking an analogy about unity and forcing it to answer an entirely different ontological question.

But the most serious problem is your claim that “Christ, the God of the Old Testament, ceased to exist.”

Scripture does NOT teach that God ceased to exist for three days.

God “only hath immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16). God did not blink out of existence on Calvary.

What died?

“The MAN Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5

Jesus possessed genuine humanity capable of suffering, bleeding, and dying. His death wasn't imaginary. His human life was genuinely surrendered and His body genuinely died.

But saying the eternal God literally ceased to exist creates an enormous contradiction: if Jesus is the God of the Old Testament, and that God ceased existing, who was sustaining creation while God didn't exist?

Hebrews 1:3 says He is “upholding all things by the word of his power.”

Even more devastating to your argument, Jesus explicitly said:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I WILL RAISE IT UP.” — John 2:19

John then explains:

“But he spake of the temple of HIS BODY.” — John 2:21

Jesus also said:

“I lay down my life, that I might TAKE IT AGAIN.” — John 10:17

And:

“I have power to lay it down, and I have power to TAKE IT AGAIN.” — John 10:18

So Scripture says the Father raised Jesus (Galatians 1:1), God raised Jesus (Acts 2:24), the Spirit raised Jesus (Romans 8:11), AND Jesus said “I will raise it up.”

Your theology requires separate divine beings to explain those statements. Scripture doesn't. The one divine Spirit raised the humanity in which He had manifested Himself.

And no, Christ's genuine bodily death does NOT mean every human being automatically pays his own penalty merely by physically dying. That's a complete non sequitur.

Christ's sacrifice has saving value because He was the sinless Lamb of God who voluntarily offered Himself for others—not because deity temporarily ceased existing.

“Christ died for our sins.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3

“Who did no sin.” — 1 Peter 2:22

“Who his own self bare our sins in his own BODY on the tree.” — 1 Peter 2:24

Notice that last word: BODY.

Peter explicitly locates the sacrificial suffering in “his own body on the tree.” Yet you're claiming that saying His body died somehow “denies Christ at the highest level.” Scripture itself says His body bore our sins!

And your interpretation of John 1 is equally problematic.

John doesn't say an eternal divine “entity” called the Word transformed Himself from spirit into a human being and ceased existing as God.

It says:

“The Word was God.” — John 1:1

Then:

“The Word was made flesh.” — John 1:14

The Greek Logos is God's Word, self-expression, reason and revelatory purpose. God's eternal Word became flesh—it was perfectly expressed and manifested in the man Jesus Christ.

That's why Paul doesn't say “one divine person became another divine person.” He says:

“God was manifest in the flesh.” — 1 Timothy 3:16

And:

“God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto HIMSELF.” — 2 Corinthians 5:19

And:

“For in him dwelleth ALL the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” — Colossians 2:9

Finally, Matthew 12:40 proves that the Son of Man truly died and was buried. It does NOT say, “The eternal God ceased to exist for three days.” You added that conclusion to the text.

The biblical picture is far more coherent:

ONE eternal God.

The Father is the eternal, invisible Spirit.

The Son is the genuine humanity conceived and born in time through which that one God manifested Himself.

The Son genuinely suffered. The Son genuinely shed blood. The Son genuinely died. The Son was genuinely buried.

And the eternal God who cannot cease being God raised that body from the grave.

That doesn't diminish Calvary.

It is precisely what makes Calvary possible:

“God was manifest in the flesh.” — 1 Timothy 3:16

The mystery isn't that one God stopped existing.

The mystery is that the immortal, invisible God came to us in genuine humanity capable of dying—and through that sinless human sacrifice accomplished our redemption.

text:
The Warrior Nation That Vanished Before Troy Was Ever Founded

Most people who know the Amazons have never heard of the ones Diodorus Siculus insists came first. He argues that a nation of warrior women ruled from Libya centuries before the more famous group settled near the river Thermodon, and that their disappearance long before the Trojan War is exactly why later writers forgot them and credited their fame to a different, better-documented group entirely.

In this account, women handled warfare and government while men ran the households and raised children, barred from military service or public office so they would never grow ambitious enough to challenge the women who ruled them. Girls born into the nation had their breasts cauterized in infancy, which Diodorus offers as the actual origin of the name Amazon. He places their homeland on an island called Hespera, inside a lake near the Atlas Mountains, describing fruit-bearing trees and herds of livestock but no cultivated grain at all.

Diodorus credits their queen, Myrina, with assembling thirty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry, armed with serpent-hide shields and bows they could fire accurately even while retreating. Her campaign leveled a city called Cerne after its defenders fled inside the walls, and the slaughter that followed was deliberate, meant to terrify neighboring towns into surrender without a fight. It worked. The Atlantians gave up their cities by treaty, and Myrina rebuilt what she had destroyed, naming the replacement city after herself.

Her next war, against the Gorgons, went less cleanly. The Amazons won the battle and took three thousand prisoners, but those captives waited for a night when the guard grew careless, seized swords, and killed a substantial number of their captors before being wiped out to the last woman. Myrina buried her own dead under three mounds that Diodorus says were still called the Amazon heaps in his own time.

The campaign kept moving after that: Egypt, Arabia, Syria, the Taurus mountains, a chain of new cities along the coast, one of them named for her sister. Diodorus reports she died fighting Thracian and Scythian exiles who invaded Amazon territory in retaliation, and that her surviving forces retreated to Libya for good after repeated defeats. He does not explain why a nation this active in his account left so little trace in anyone else's.

"Venezuela's mineral wealth remains largely unproven
Country suffers from outdated data, weak infrastructure and illegal mining
Caracas is seeking foreign investment as Washington looks to deepen its economic influence
Trump is trying to reshape Venezuela's oil industry and broader resource sector.

 The Trump administration is seeking greater U.S. access to Venezuela's minerals, including gold, as it expands its push to gain control and influence over the South ​American country's vast natural resources beyond oil, according to three sources familiar with the discussions.

With its enormous oil reserves ​and potentially significant deposits of gold and other minerals, Venezuela offers the Trump administration an opportunity to tie resource access to its national security and economic agenda.
The administration has already taken steps to open Venezuela's minerals ​sector to U.S. business.
In March, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control authorized certain transactions involving Venezuelan-origin gold, including activities tied to state-owned gold miner Minerven. Later that month, Treasury broadened the authorization to cover Venezuelan-origin minerals, ‌including gold, while ⁠allowing some mining-related services and negotiations of potential investment contracts.

The moves have created a framework for U.S. companies to pursue opportunities in Venezuela's mining sector as the administration seeks to revive investment while expanding U.S. sway over the country's oil industry.
Trump already has moved aggressively to reshape Venezuela's oil industry. Last week, he announced a deal under which the U.S. would take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves, although the precise legal structure of that arrangement has not been disclosed.
There are, however, fears within Venezuela that Trump is turning the country into a modern-day colony.

FURTHER STUDY OF MINERAL RESOURCES NEEDED
Venezuela's mineral potential remains difficult to ​assess because much of its geological data is outdated ​and illegal groups control gold deposits in the ⁠Orinoco Mining Arc, a vast area near the country's borders with Guyana and Brazil.
While Venezuela has produced gold, iron ore, bauxite and nickel, mining companies and investors are likely to seek updated geological studies before making significant new investments, analysts have said, given the uncertainty surrounding its mineral estimates, weak infrastructure and pervasive illegal ​mining.

A 2018 Venezuelan government report estimated the country's resources at 644 metric tons of gold, 14.68 billion metric tons of iron ore, 321.5 million metric tons of bauxite and 407,885 metric tons of nickel. But the report used terms such as "reserve" and "resource" interchangeably, making it difficult to determine how much could be economically extracted.
A 2021 ⁠Venezuelan government map, ​based on data compiled in 2009, identified deposits of numerous other minerals, including copper, nickel, coltan, uranium and tungsten, but did ​not provide volumes.
The country does not appear to have sizeable reserves of rare earths, which are used in magnets and other advanced technologies.
Venezuelan lawmakers in April unanimously approved a mining law aimed at spurring new investment. It dictated that mineral deposits remain the property of ​the government and set a royalty tax of up to 13% of the gross production value of a mineral."
