text:
CanaryMedia: "Virginia to cut rooftop solar costs with nation-first bulk-buy program," by Elizabeth Ouzts.

"Last month, Virginia became the first state...to launch a bulk-purchasing campaign for rooftop solar—a move that promises to bring down the cost of installing panels for households across Old Dominion." Idea behind the program, called Switch Together, is simple: Solar panels come cheaper by the dozen, like that old Disney movie. "Trusted [+ vetted] solar installers can pool demand to purchase equipment in bulk + pass the discounts on to participants." Solar United Neighbors [SUN], the nonprofit running the initiative, is expanding statewide in Virginia at the urging of the office of Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, who is looking for ways to lower energy bills as utilities jack up rates in the world’s data center capital.

"If more people go solar, that’s less strain on the grid, and there’s less need to build costly infrastructure that the entire rate base would actually pay for," said Brandon Praileau, SUN’s Virginia program director, who joined the group in 2023 after rooftop solar helped his church in Norfolk cut utility bills by a quarter. "The state is not providing any funding for Switch Together, though its partnership promises to amplify the reach of the bulk-purchasing effort, which is focused on solar but also offers residents access to cheaper home batteries, EV chargers, and, in some locations, heat pumps."

By the time this year's bulk-purchasing drive is over, Praileau expects those figures will swell to 5,000 requests for info and about 500 signed contracts. "We’re talking about a utility-scale amount of solar with those numbers...almost 4 megawatts [MW].” The rooftop panels are expected to cut $2,200 off the average annual utility bill.

Exactly how much households save on installation varies across the state, but it ranges from 20% to 30% off—vital discounts after Trump + Republicans in Congress killed the 30% federal tax credit for households investing in renewable energy.

"Rooftop solar both slashes power costs for homes that install it and can drive down expenses for utility customers at large." We should help the Sun shine in.

text:
The thing most people do wrong when they try to increase AOV is only thinking about price, bundles, & upsells.

That’s 50% of it. 

& if you only focus on those (especially price) there’s a big chance you’ll decrease CVR more than you increase AOV.

The unsexy thing that actually increase AOV the most is increasing perceived value.

It’s pretty simple once you understand it so I’m gonna break down the 3 biggest levers you can pull here:

1. Market to a bigger emotion

The more painful/desirable the emotion you’re marketing to, the more you can charge. If you can, always tie your offer to either gaining more status, avoiding pain, belonging in a group, or reproduction/attracting the opposite sex. Most of you can do this. The example I always use here is a testosterone supplement we marketed as “the hidden advantage that let’s guys attract 10/10 women without trying”. We featured this angle in ads, pre-sell pages, & the PDP.

2. Offer the complete solution to that bigger emotion

Once you’re marketing to a bigger emotion, you want to frame your product as “everything you need to achieve that”. This is where the actual power of bundles lie. Bundle together SKUs that together get the customer that big outcome (like attracting 10/10 women), & then in your pre-sell pages & on your PDP, you explain how the products work together to get that result & why that combination of products is superior.

3. Root cause education & unique mechanisms

If there’s even something remotely unique about HOW your product/bundle gets the customer the result (like a unique ingredient or tech), do this:

- on your pre-sell pages, break down the root cause to the problem the prospect has (& make sure the problem you reveal is something this unique thing about your product solves)
- explain why other solutions (your competitors) don’t solve this root cause
- explain what’s needed to solve it (your unique thing, but don’t mention your product, just explain what the solution is)
- then you present your product & how it is that solution

This makes you far less comparable to competitors, allowing you to charge more because you’re “delivering the ACTUAL solution & no one else is doing that”

These 3 things are the 80/20 of increasing perceived value, which in turn is like 50% of increasing AOV without killing CVR.

Now go & outbid your competitors.

text:
Caring for a parent with dementia is a grief like no other. You are mourning someone who is still here, losing them a piece at a time, often feeling completely and utterly alone. People bring meals when someone passes, but rarely does anyone know what to offer for a sorrow that has no funeral and no end in sight.

When the weariness presses down and you have almost nothing left, you don't need a heavy instruction manual. You need a gentle lifeline. You need to know that when the fog rolls in, grace does not roll out—it is nearest right there in the mist. 

📖 **"Grace in the Fog"** by Ruth Ellen Abbott is an accessible digital companion providing 40 short daily devotions crafted specifically for the exact moments when your own words have run dry. Read it in the quiet five minutes before they wake, or during the long evening after they finally sleep.

Here is what you will find inside these pages:
🕊️ **Grief:** Faithful guidance for coping with anticipatory grief, mourning a living loss while trusting the God who keeps your tears.
⏳ **Patience:** Divine strength for the long road of caregiving, taking it one steady, grace-filled day at a time.
🤍 **Identity:** A reminder of the eternal soul that remains beautifully intact beneath the fading memories and medical symptoms.
🛌 **Rest:** Biblical peace for the weary and burdened who cannot physically stop their relentless caregiving duties.
✨ **Hope & Presence:** Unfailing spiritual support to help you cling to the light the darkness cannot overcome.

🚨 **The Practical Tool You Need Today:** 
There are no rigid rules here. Read one devotion a day, one a week, or three in a difficult middle-of-the-night hour. Each day offers a comforting verse to hold, a word of deep spiritual encouragement, and a short guided prayer for when you simply cannot pray anymore. 

👇 Get your digital copy and find the comfort you deserve today:

By Anthony Daniel

There are moments in the political history of a developing republic when institutional amnesia threatens to permanently bury the truth, allowing those who allegedly pillaged public coffers to posture unbothered as democratic statesmen. 

This is precisely the moral, legal, and systemic hazard confronting Nigeria regarding former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. For two decades, a monumental act of public resource diversion has sat in plain sight on the highbrow tarmac of Abuja’s premier commercial district. 

No. 555 Adetokunbo Ademola Crescent—historically tied to the controversial National Dynamic Television (NDTV) project and subsequently converted into a permanent, high-security political sanctuary—stands as a stark, concrete monument to administrative betrayal, public fund manipulation, and unpunished executive grandstanding.

It is past time for the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to wake from its institutional slumber, step into the breach, and reclaim this asset for the Federal Government of Nigeria.

The foundational anatomy of this sordid transaction is etched indelibly into official state records, most notably the damning, comprehensive 21-page EFCC investigative dossier released in September 2006. That report laid bare an ecosystem of self-indicting rationalizations and defensive maneuvers offered by the former Vice President when he was pressed to explain how state resources under the Petroleum Technology Development Fund (PTDF) were managed under his direct supervision. 

Confronted with the unlawful placement of public funds from the PTDF into Equatorial Trust Bank (ETB), Atiku offered an explanation dripping with unvarnished executive arrogance. He defended the placement as a product of "his judgement on the safety of the investment on maturity and the reasonableness of the returns on investment, bearing in mind what obtained in the industry at the material time."

Yet, this calculated defense revealed a glaring, guilty evasion. As the EFCC report sharply noted, His Excellency maintained a deafening, convenient silence regarding parallel, massive placements in Trans International Bank (TIB). When interrogated about the staggering movement of funds siphoned directly from the PTDF accounts, Atiku suffered a sudden, selective memory collapse, stating defensively that he could not remember the circumstances surrounding the movement of millions to ETB, neither could he recollect giving explicit, due-process approval for such explosive financial shifts.

Worse still was the sordid paper trail of corruption leading directly to bricks, mortar, and private corporate control. The initial payment of 30 million Naira for the acquisition of No. 555 Adetokunbo Ademola Crescent—funneled toward the establishment of the NDTV Headquarters and subsequently converted into Atiku's permanent political headquarters—exposed the direct, unconscionable nexus between public trust and private enrichment.

text: “1950, a street in the fog” by Oliver R closes the quadriptych like a night that does not end: it fades away.The fourth and final painting of the 1950 series takes up exactly the composition of the first panel, 1950, a street under the moon. Same street, same buildings, same receding perspective, same possible silhouettes. Nothing has moved. Only the fog has entered. It does not arrive as a meteorological accident. It is the artist’s final gesture. Where the moon of the first painting still carved out volumes, drew sharp shadows and offered the night an almost metaphysical clarity, the fog of this fourth panel absorbs everything. The façades dissolve. The roofs no longer have contours. The light of the street lamps, once precise, becomes a milky, iridescent, almost religious halo. The moon itself is no more than a paler stain in the mist, a memory of light.Oliver R is not painting a simple change of atmosphere. He is painting the end of a cycle. The fog is not merely climatic; it is temporal. It envelops “the end of the night” the way one closes a book. It is no longer the hour of lunar insomnia, nor the hour of waiting. It is the hour when the night itself grows weary, when forms abandon their identity and the city of 1950 begins to slip out of time.The colours, already restrained in the first painting, are reduced here to an extremely sober range: bluish greys, extinguished ochres, golds dulled by humidity. The pavement, which once reflected the moon with an almost photographic sharpness, now offers only indistinct glimmers. Everything becomes suggestion. A period car, if it exists, is no longer more than a possible presence, a ghost that the gaze reconstitutes more than it sees.This formal economy is characteristic of Oliver R. As in Les Parisiennes or Inaccessible, the artist refuses the spectacular. He prefers silence. Here, the silence is muffled. Footsteps can no longer be heard. The wind can no longer be heard. Even time can no longer be heard. The fog has stifled everything, including the narrative.The 1950 quadriptych therefore closes on an image of erasure. After the lunar clarity of the first painting, after the two intermediate panels that no doubt explored other states of this same street, Oliver R chooses not to open the day. He lets the night lose itself in its own vapour. 1950 does not wake up. It evaporates.This may be the series’ finest decision. By plunging the identical scene into fog, the artist does not repeat: he concludes. He transforms a precise place into memory. It is no longer a street. It is the memory of a street. And memory, like fog, has no definitive contours.1950, a street in the fog is not one more painting. It is the moment when the quadriptych accepts to disappear. The night is over, but day has not yet arrived. There is only this mist, thick, soft and definitive, covering everything that has been seen since the first painting.The series ends in silence. And that is exactly how it had to end. It is printed on art paper, mounted on a 0.3 cm dibond support, set in a reinforced frame and protected by 0.5 cm anti-reflective plexiglass. A unique piece, it comes with a digital certificate.

China is emerging as a favored destination for overseas cancer patients seeking CAR-T therapy due to lower costs and biotech innovation.View moreSHANGHAI—Michael Walters, 25, had just begun his first full-time job out of university when he was diagnosed last year with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a blood cancer.Walters, who hails from New Zealand, underwent several unsuccessful rounds of chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy in Auckland. Then doctors told him about CAR-T treatment, in which a patient’s immune cells are extracted, re-engineered in a laboratory and reintroduced into the body to fight cancer cells.Walters looked at the U.S. and India as well as Australia, where a hospital in Melbourne said it could treat him with the therapy—at a cost of as much as $600,000, a prohibitive sum for his https://t.co/xVOk6rlOW1 SinoUnited Hospital in Shanghai, Walters paid less than half that amount—and, on Aug. 18, learned that the treatment had succeeded in pushing his lymphoma into complete remission.“I feel more appreciative of life,” Walters said. “If this was 10 or 15 years ago, I wouldn’t have this option.”CAR-T therapy, short for chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, was pioneered in the U.S. Today, however, Shanghai is emerging as a favored destination for patients from America and other rich countries—a testament not only to China’s low costs but also to the country’s emergence as an innovator in biotechnology.CAR-T cell therapy
📷12Draw patients' blood to obtain T-cellsEngineer CAR-T cells in a laboratoryChimeric antigenreceptor (CAR)Insert gene for CART-cell3Grow millions of CAR-T cellsCAR-T cells bind to cancerous cells and fight themReintroduce lab-engineered CAR-T cells into patient54Cancer cellSource: National Cancer InstituteRoque Ruiz/WSJ“China has basically done to CAR-T cell therapy the same thing that it’s done to other industries, which is, they’ve industrialized it,” said Sairah Ahmed, director of the CAR-T program in the department of lymphoma and myeloma at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in https://t.co/peKJR4zXL0 some cases, China has jumped ahead of the U.S. In June, Beijing regulators greenlighted a CAR-T treatment for a cancer of the stomach and upper small intestine—the world’s first approved CAR-T therapy for solid tumors.Josh Bronkhorst, the 59-year-old chief executive of a financial services company, was among the first to get the treatment after approval. Diagnosed in December, he went through four months of chemotherapy and immunotherapy—only to find that the tumor was still growing.His doctors told him another round of chemotherapy would have only a 15% chance of success. So Bronkhorst, also a New Zealander, headed to China.“Every day is getting better,” Bronkhorst said in a faint voice on Aug. 6 from his bed at Jiahui International Hospital in Shanghai. By then, 10 days after the re-engineered cells were infused into his body, the buildup of extra fluids caused by Bronkhorst’s cancer had come to a halt, allowing doctors to remove a drainage tube.“It’s not a miracle drug, but this was by far the best option I could find,” he said at the time.On Aug. 16, he flew back to New Zealand, where he continues to recover.Josh Bronkhorst underwent CAR-T treatment for stomach cancer at Jiahui International Hospital in Shanghai. JIAHUI INTERNATIONAL HOSPITAL📷
Ahmed of MD Anderson said she has advised some of her overseas patients to seek treatment in China, where CAR-T therapy can range between $150,000 and $230,000, versus $550,000 to $850,000 in the U.S.Regulators in dozens of countries have approved CAR-T therapy for blood cancers, including leukemia, lymphoma and myeloma. The therapies Bronkhorst and Walters received are among nine CAR-T products approved by Chinese regulators, the most in the world.Bronkhorst’s stomach-cancer treatment was developed by Shanghai-based CARsgen Therapeutics, which won Chinese approval for the solid tumor CAR-T therapy following a clinical-trial program that included U.S. patients at MD Anderson and Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.Advertisement“We have more and more new weapons to fight cancer,” Li Zonghai, founder and chief executive of CARsgen, said in an interview. “A lot of people said we couldn’t treat it, and now there are more and more modalities—so many treatment options.”For all of its advances, China has also found itself in controversy over the transparency of its clinical trials, after three people, including a 6-year-old girl, were reported to have died while receiving experimental medicines. In general, Chinese regulators allow hospitals to start clinical trials with less central government oversight than the U.S. requires—a system that has enabled innovation but also increased risks for patients in https://t.co/ao03tz07T3 contrast, China’s private international hospitals have generally been more cautious, steering clear of clinical trials and sticking only to therapies, including CAR-T treatments, that have been approved by regulators for commercialization.Treatment pamphlets, patient photos and letters at Shanghai SinoUnited Hospital.📷
Harnessing the immune system to attack cancer is the principle behind many of this century’s medical advances, and the pace is https://t.co/7jTxdhedI3 August, Cambridge, Mass.-based Moderna and its partner Merck said their mRNA-based vaccine succeeded in preventing cancer from coming back or spreading in high-risk melanoma patients. The potential breakthrough could extend the lifespans of hundreds of thousands of people with the deadly skin cancer.Meanwhile, the Food and Drug Administration last month approved a therapy for pancreatic tumors, a breakthrough in fighting one of the deadliest forms of cancer.Chinese regulators first granted approval for CAR-T therapy to be administered to overseas patients in 2021. Since it began offering CAR-T in 2023, Shanghai SinoUnited Hospital has treated roughly three dozen patients from 12 countries, said Dr. Kathy Shi, the hospital’s founder and chief executive. Shi, a cardiologist who did her postdoctoral work at Emory University in Atlanta, said most of them were now cancer-free.Dr. Kathy Shi, left, is the president of Shanghai SinoUnited Hospital, which began offering CAR-T in 2023.📷
As word has spread, SinoUnited Hospital says it has welcomed patients from MD Anderson, Mayo Clinic and Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. Shi says the hospital has also seen an uptick in inquiries from across the U.S., Canada, Europe and Southeast Asia.“A year ago, I was frequently talking to Chinese patients seeking international treatment,” said Xuan Linli, chief of medical oncology at Jiahui Hospital. “Now, more and more overseas patients are requesting consultations with us.”CAR-T therapies have been studied in the U.S. since the 1980s and in China since the 1990s. A breakthrough came in 2012 when Pennsylvania native Emily Whitehead, then 6 years old, became the first child to beat leukemia after undergoing the therapy. (She is now an undergraduate at the University of Pennsylvania, steps from where she received her CAR-T treatment.)CAR-T remains a niche within cancer treatment because it can treat a limited number of cancer types. For now, CAR-T treatment generally comes only after other treatments have failed, in part because of potential side effects such as inflammation caused by the infusion.Patients choose China not merely for the low cost of treatment, but because the country’s international hospitals offer a range of services—a critical factor, since CAR-T therapy can require intensive care and intervention from cardiologists, neurologists and other specialists.CAR-T therapy for blood cancers has been approved in dozens of countries.📷
Because CAR-T requires tailor-made cellular therapy for each patient, China’s ability to crank out the therapies in a matter of days—in laboratories just a short drive from Shanghai—can give it an edge over countries where the wait is longer.The possibility of immediate treatment in China makes it an attractive choice for patients fighting aggressive cancers.Bronkhorst and Walters also describe better customer service than they found when considering other countries, including help in securing medical visas and a higher level of English-language proficiency.Walters said he was reassured when he got on a video call with SinoUnited Hospital hematologist Lily Zhou, who did her postdoctoral work at the University of California, San https://t.co/3P1ps6Taqo New Zealand, “I felt like I had done more research and knew more about it than the doctors I was talking to,” Walters said. “But she has so much experience.…It was nice to talk to someone who knew exactly what she was doing.”Walters and his friends started a crowdfunding effort online to cover most of the costs, and in late June he flew to Shanghai to begin his treatment under Zhou. It was his first time traveling there. On his 25th birthday, the staff at SinoUnited Hospital presented him with a cake.For his next birthday, he is planning to be home in Auckland, with his cancer still in remission.“I’d give anything to be healthy right now,” Walters said. “I want to be able to worry about the normal everyday things that everyone worries about: university, work, girlfriends, gossip.”Zhao Yueling contributed to this article.Copyright ©2026 Dow Jones & Company, Inc. Strength means being able to sustain the response, support affected workers and offer a clear path to removing tariffs on both sides.

The objective is a workable agreement that respects Canada’s sovereignty. Matching every escalation indefinitely would become a costly substitute for achieving one.

text:
Ezra Levant: Canada already has the 'trusted news' list the U.S. just warned Britain about 🇨🇦

A letter was published this week by the United States Embassy in London, addressed to the British government, all about what you are doing right now: watching news the government didn't pick for you.

On Friday's episode of The Ezra Levant Show, @ezralevant weighed in on the U.S. government formally telling Britain that ranking "trusted news" at the top of your feed is censorship — and how Canada has been doing it for years.

A letter was published this week by the United States Embassy in London, addressed to the British government, all about what you are doing right now: watching news the government didn't pick for you.

Here's the background. On June 23, Britain's culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, put out a green paper — a discussion document, a trial balloon, cheekily titled “Watch this Space.” Her idea was that Britain's public service broadcasters — the BBC, ITV, Channel 4, Channel 5 — should be made “prominent and easy to find” on platforms like YouTube. Prominent means, in the government's own words, more likely to sit at the top of a person's social media feed. The BBC goes to the top, and then, in the government's phrasing, “other trustworthy providers.”

Who qualifies as trustworthy? The paper doesn't say. Who decides? It doesn't say that either.

Ezra guessed that "trustworthy providers" means reporters politicians trust — not reporters the people trust. There's a difference.

The government cites an Ofcom figure to justify the plan: 75 percent of young people aged 16 to 24 get their news from social media, not from the BBC. To a government that owns a broadcaster, that Ofcom number is a threat. But the fix on offer isn't a better BBC; it's an algorithm rigged so the BBC shows up whether viewers want it or not.

YouTube saw it immediately. In July, the platform warned British creators the rules could force it to “put some channels above others,” and urged them to write to the consultation. Ezra isn't in the habit of defending YouTube — it has demonetized Rebel News, throttled it, and pulled its videos. But even YouTube can see that ordering it to put the BBC on top means somebody else goes to the bottom. By YouTube's own accounting, British creators are worth more than £2 billion a year to the UK economy and 45,000 jobs. Those are the people who'd be pushed down the list.

The consultation closed August 31. That's where it gets interesting.

On July 14, Jim Jordan, chairman of the U.S. House Judiciary Committee, wrote directly to Lisa Nandy. His letter described the plan as creating “a tiered information system in which media outlets that are supported and legitimized by the British government are at the top,” a form of gatekeeping, he wrote, that stifles independent and smaller outlets. He demanded a briefing.

That was a congressman speaking. Then came the executive branch.

On September 2, the U.S. Embassy in London filed the formal position of the American government in the British consultation. It states plainly that Washington has “serious concerns” about the plan, and that a government picking which outlets get preferential visibility “risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.”

Then comes the line Ezra wanted read twice: “the effect on a government-disfavored speaker or media source's reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal.” Not meaningfully different than outright removal. In other words: bury someone in the algorithm, and you've censored them, full stop. No need to delete the channel, just make sure nobody sees it.

The U.S. government says it would “likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship,” and warns it “could establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content.” Washington's ask is not to amend the plan. It's to withdraw it entirely.

Then come the questions — and Ezra has been asking versions of every one of them in Canada for four years. What criteria decide whether an outlet is “sufficiently trustworthy”? Who makes that call? Will the criteria be public? Is there an appeal for outlets left off the list? And what role do third-party “media literacy” groups — the fact-checkers — play in deciding who gets ranked?

Good questions, every one. Canada already answered them, years ago, and the answer was always the same: the government decides, and if an outlet doesn't like it, see it in court.

Canada doesn't call it a trust list. It's called a Qualified Canadian Journalism Organization (QCJO), and it functions as a journalism licence. Hold one, and a newsroom's payroll is subsidized, and its subscribers get a tax credit. Don't hold one, and it's shut out. The committee that decides is appointed — by the government, not by the public. When Rebel News, one of the largest independent news organizations in the country, applied, Trudeau's committee ruled that less than two per cent of what we do qualifies as “original news,” and labelled us “activists.”

Ezra has made this point before, and he made it again: it is anathema to a free press for a government committee to determine who is or isn't a journalist.

Real democracies don't issue journalism licences. Russia does. Iran does. China does.

Rebel News sued. In September 2024, the Federal Court sided with the CRA — a result Ezra found frankly shocking. Rebel News appealed. Last September, in the Federal Court of Appeal in Toronto, a lawyer for Mark Carney's government told three judges the whole point of the system is to make sure Canadians get journalism that is “informed and reliable.” A ruling is still pending, and Ezra isn't optimistic — this is Canada in 2026, after all.

So the government decides who is informed, reliable, trustworthy and, ultimately, who is approved.

Set the two side by side. Britain proposes a list of government-approved news, and the Americans file a formal objection calling it censorship. Canada built a list of government-approved news, enforced it through the tax code, fought a newsroom in court for four years to keep it, then layered on a second mechanism at the CRTC — and the American response has so far focused on unfair trade practices. Fair concern. But what about the freedom part?

What Britain is only contemplating, Canada has already been doing to Rebel News, and to every genuinely independent outlet in the country — exactly what the U.S. just told Britain not to start.

At least Britain's government had the decency to run a public consultation, and got told off by its closest ally for the trouble. Canada never asked anybody. A government committee simply decided Rebel News isn't journalism, and left us to spend more than $177,000 fighting that decision in court.

Ask who makes the “trusted” list in Canada. The outlets on the payroll: the CBC, with its billion dollars a year; the newspapers cashing subsidy cheques. Ask who's left off it: the outlets that won't take the government's money.

Trustworthy, it turns out, means paid for.

text:
She gave her name as Margo. Five minutes later the woman who had hired her off a Bronx street corner was calling her Margie, and by the end of the day she was calling her Mary. Marvel Cooke scrubbed that apartment's linoleum on her hands and knees and was paid three dollars and forty cents by the clock on that woman's wall, twenty cents short of her own carfare home.

On those same corners in 1935, fifteen cents bought an hour of a woman's life.

The hour was the part they stole.

They called it the Bronx slave market, and it was not one corner. The two where the bidding ran heaviest sat at 167th Street and Jerome Avenue and at Simpson and Westchester Avenues, and Marvel Cooke, looking back on it fifteen years later, put the number across the whole borough at twenty or thirty.

Black women stood on those corners and waited for white housewives to buy them by the hour.

Baker and Cooke put the going rates on paper. Fifteen cents an hour, twenty, twenty-five, and thirty if a woman was lucky.

They came as early as eight in the morning. Some were still standing there at one in the afternoon with nothing.

Rain or shine, cold or hot. Old women and young women, some worn down and some carefully dressed, and every last one of them holding a paper bag.

The bag held her work clothes. It was how you could tell, from across a street, what a woman was standing there for.

Most of them rode down from Harlem on the train. The ones who did not have the nickel for the fare walked it.

At Jerome Avenue there were benches around a green square, and Ella Baker and Marvel Cooke called that the more humane of the two markets for exactly that reason. The women there had somewhere to sit.

At Simpson Avenue there was nothing. The women leaned against store fronts and lamp posts, or they went up and down the block hunting for a discarded box to drag over and rest on.

That is the whole difference between the two corners, and it is worth holding onto. One had benches and the other had garbage.

Before 1929 most of these women had been working. Some had held steady places in the big houses in the rich Eighties, or out in Westchester and on Long Island, at wages that covered a life.

Then the crash came. The woman who had employed them either started doing her own floors or fired the Black worker to hire a white one who had just been let out of something better.

The employment agencies took a fee whether or not they placed you, and they placed white women first. Relief was thin and slow and came with a caseworker attached to it.

So the corner. Not because it promised anything, Baker and Cooke wrote, but because a woman in that position had run out of doors.

The crash also produced a brand new class of employer. The lower middle class housewife who had never in her life been able to afford help could suddenly have a woman on her knees scrubbing linoleum for a quarter.

The buyer walked the line looking the women over. Cooke wrote that she all but undressed them with her eyes, measuring how much work each one looked able to stand.

Then she asked the price and beat it down as far as the woman would let her. The figure they landed on was always below what the agencies asked and below what the women had agreed among themselves.

What got bought was heavy. Floors scrubbed on the knees, tubs of blankets and furniture covers, mattresses beaten, walls washed down, a week of laundry crammed into a day.

The job every one of them dreaded was windows. In a Bronx apartment house that meant sitting out on the ledge with the top sash pulled down across your lap and the street underneath you.

One woman was badly hurt falling from a sixth floor window. Another woman fell and died.

The Domestic Workers Union eventually wrote a contract that simply banned the task outright.

In September 1935 a woman named Millie Jones sat down to lunch with two strangers on Simpson Avenue and told them what a week of it actually came to.

She had worked in the neighborhood for five dollars a week and carfare. The apartment had six rooms and fifteen windows, and every single week she washed all fifteen of them.

If her employer found one speck on one pane, Millie Jones did the window again.

Mondays she washed. Tuesdays she finished whatever ironing Monday had not swallowed, and with a husband and two grown sons in that house it came to twenty-one shirts a week, ten sheets, and at least two blankets.

Every floor in the place got washed and waxed on her hands and knees, every week. Two or three times a week she stripped the covers off all the furniture and beat the mattresses.

One of the sons put his hands on her. She said fighting him off left her about as tired as the work did.

She lasted five weeks. Then she asked for one Sunday off, because her boyfriend was coming up from Washington on an excursion train, and she was told that if she did not come in on Sunday she need not come in again.

She did not go back. That is how she ended up on a corner in the Bronx.

The day before she met the two strangers she had not had a cent in her pocket and took the first thing offered. She went to work at eleven in the morning and finished at five, washing windows, scrubbing floors, and cleaning the baby's soiled laundry.

She said she had been surprised to be fed at all, because plenty of them gave you nothing.

At the end of it she was handed thirty-five cents. Her employer explained that a quarter had been taken out for the lunch.

Six hours. Millie Jones did the arithmetic out loud at the table, and the number she came to was ten cents an hour.

That was the ordinary shape of the theft, and it hardly ever touched the price agreed on the sidewalk.

The clock got turned back an hour while the woman was in another room. Work got criticized at the end of the day so the full amount would not have to be handed over.

More got piled on than had been bargained for. Some days a woman worked the whole day through and was sent home with nothing at all.

The rate was public and the hours were private, and every person in that market understood which of the two was worth stealing.

The two strangers who bought Millie Jones that lunch had come off the train at Simpson and Westchester on the morning of 14 September 1935, carrying beat-up bags and dressed to look like they had nothing.

Ella Baker was a Harlem organizer who had spent the early thirties building Black consumer cooperatives. Marvel Cooke was a newspaperwoman who had come up through The Crisis as W. E. B. Du Bois's assistant.

They took a position outside the flower shop on the corner and waited to be bought.

The shop window behind them had gardenias in it, and roses, and the first chrysanthemums of the season. All of it priced, all of it reasonable.

It took almost no time at all. A woman came up, looked the two of them over, asked what they worked for, and walked off the instant they asked what she paid.

She was bargaining with a stronger woman by the lamp post within the minute, and she led her away down a side street two blocks off.

The other women on the corner did not trust the newcomers. Then it began to rain and a dozen of them crowded into the five and ten doorway together, and after that the talking came easier.

A West Indian woman who had spent the morning patrolling the block, all but daring somebody not to hire her, hushed the group so the store manager would not push them all back out into the wet.

They finished the conversation in whispers under the awning.

A man in plain clothes had been trailing the two reporters for a while by then, waiting for a chance to run them in for soliciting. When they split up he lost them, and when they stood together he grinned and winked.

An elderly couple came looking for somebody to send up to their daughter's place on Jerome Avenue. The husband said twenty-five cents an hour and the wife scowled and said twenty, and they explained that the carfare would be paid once she got there.

Five or six women turned them down flat.

And on an upturned soap box sat a woman who had already lined up work for the next day and could afford to be choosy.

She had watched the old couple strike out and was pleased about it. When a fresh group came down the elevated steps and started underselling the corner, she said those were the ones who made it bad for everybody, and that the corner had run them off once already the week before.

Then she said somebody ought to organize them or something.

She said it sitting on a box she had pulled off the street because there was nowhere else to sit, and she said it as though it were somebody else's job.

It was not somebody else's job. It was already happening on that block.

By that autumn the Simpson Avenue corner had a rough union of its own, with no charter, no dues and no name.

Women who took less than thirty cents an hour got run off. For the holiday that year the regulars held together and refused to go out for less than thirty-five.

That is a wage floor, set on a sidewalk, by women who had no legal right to one. Congress had written domestic workers out of the Social Security Act that August and out of the labor relations act that July.

When the federal wage and hour law arrived in 1938, they were left out of that as well.

Dora Jones and Rosa Rayside were building the Domestic Workers Union, Local 149, through those same years. By 1937 it ran somewhere between three hundred and fifty and a thousand members and it opened a free hiring hall on White Plains Road.

Jones could never crack the street corners. The women out there told her they did better on the sidewalk than at any agency, and she was blunt about how hard they were to reach.

The union organized in the only way that was available to it, which was one woman at a time, on foot, outside churches and subway entrances, in the hours after a full day of somebody else's floors.

In the autumn of 1949 it ran a course in Negro history. A union down to a hundred and twenty-five paid-up members had decided that the way to reach exhausted women was to teach them their own history, and it brought in new members.

Nina Evans, who was running Local 149 by then, said the aim was for Black workers to walk erect, in dignity and pride, alongside their white allies.

Thirteen years before that course, Louise Thompson Patterson had published an essay that used these corners as its evidence and put a phrase into print that nobody had used before. She wrote that Black women were exploited three times over, as workers, as women, and as Black people.

In 1937 the Amsterdam News reprinted a version of the Baker and Cooke report for Harlem readers.

In 1938 a Federal Writers' Project worker named Vivian Morris put on old clothes and went to the corners herself. On 6 December that year she sat down with a woman named Minnie Marshall, and two of Morris's manuscripts are still held at the Library of Congress, one of them titled simply Price War in the Bronx Slave Market.

In 1939 a Columbia graduate student named Lois Taylor did the same thing and stayed with it for months. Her fieldwork became her master's thesis in 1940.

In 1937, two years before Taylor started, a photographer named Robert McNeill walked up to those corners with a camera.

He was nineteen. He had left a pre-med course at Howard University the year before, enrolled at the New York Institute of Photography, and gone out to shoot the Bronx market as part of a series on Black domestic workers.

He was shooting it for Fortune magazine, and Fortune turned the pictures down.

They ran instead in Flash, a magazine for Black readers, as a thirteen photograph feature.

One of those photographs is in the Smithsonian American Art Museum. It shows women standing on the corner at 170th Street waiting for somebody to buy an hour of their time, and the title comes off the movie poster on the wall behind them, which is advertising a picture to people with an afternoon to spare.

The negatives are at the Library of Congress, catalogued as the Bronx slave market, 1937 to 1938. Two Black women waiting for day labor, and a third woman, probably white, standing there talking terms with them.

Their faces are in that frame. Not one of them has a name attached.

In 1937, the same year McNeill was shooting, a domestic worker named Pansy Kennedy sued her employer for ten dollars and sixty cents in unpaid wages, and she won.

The magistrate who heard it, F. Anthony Burke, used the occasion to announce from the bench that domestic workers were living it up on relief money and had no real interest in working. Several papers ran with it in July 1938, and Marvel Cooke answered it in the Amsterdam News nine days later.

In the autumn of 1939 a worker named Bessie Brown was hospitalized after her employers, a wealthy white couple in Mount Vernon, attacked her when she refused to leave their house without her wages.

She sued them for assault, with help from the International Labor Defense, and she lost. The not guilty verdict was read out to a packed courthouse, and afterward she said she was glad she had done it, because it had put the conditions in front of people who would otherwise never have heard of them.

By December 1939 the state was finally paying attention. Frieda Miller, New York's industrial commissioner, set up a Committee on Street Corner Markets and put Dora Jones on it.

The committee reported in June 1940 and recommended two free employment agencies for the Bronx.

Then nothing happened for eight months.

On 26 February 1941, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia ran his own investigation.

He did not announce it. He sent the police, with the Welfare Department helping, out to the corners.

They collected the women. Accounts of how many differ, with about a hundred in one telling and sixty-four in the Herald Tribune's.

Some of the women understood there was work in it. Others were told there was a day's pay and a meal in it if they would act as witnesses.

They were taken to relief centers and questioned for hours.

A great deal of that questioning was about whether they were collecting home relief.

A market existed in which Black women were bought by the hour and robbed of their time, and the city's answer was to send police to gather up the women and interrogate them about their finances.

Every person collected that morning was somebody looking for work.

The American Civil Liberties Union condemned it, and so did the National Negro Congress.

Dora Jones called it an act of terror.

La Guardia said the women had come voluntarily and that the surprise had been necessary to get truthful answers.

Weeks later the finding came out. The city had determined that no exploitation was taking place on the Bronx slave market, because the women it questioned were being paid thirty-five cents an hour and not ten.

The city had reduced the entire question to the hourly rate. It had thirty-five cents in one column, and years of documented testimony about turned-back clocks, unpaid hours and work piled past the bargain in no column at all.

The report's recommendation was the same two employment agencies the committee had already asked for a year earlier.

One true thing did come out of those interrogations, and it demolished a lie. Almost none of the women picked up that morning were on home relief.

The magistrate's speech from the bench had been wrong, and it was the mayor's own police work that proved it. Nobody went back and told the papers that had printed it.

The Simpson Day Worker Center opened at 1029 Simpson Street on 1 May 1941. Free, indoors, out of the weather, a few steps from the corner where Baker and Cooke had stood six years before.

The Militant ran a headline on it that has never been improved. The Bronx slave market, it said, had merely been moved indoors.

That was accurate. The bidding went on in there, warmer and drier, and what passed between an employer and a worker was not closely watched.

By that September the committee reported six thousand placements in five months and called it a success.

What actually emptied the corners was not the city. It was the war, which pulled labor into the factories and paid for it properly.

Then the war ended, the factory work went, and the women came back.

Marvel Cooke went back too, alone, in the last days of 1949.

She stood in front of the Woolworth's on 170th Street between Jerome and Walton Avenues with her own paper bag, and the women gathered around her the way they had fifteen years earlier.

Backs pressed to the store glass, bags held in front of them. Staring out into the street.

The rate was seventy-five cents an hour now, and set against what milk and bread and meat had done in that decade it came to almost no gain at all.

The first job she took, she quit. A woman hired her outside the Woolworth's at eighty cents an hour and walked her up Townsend Avenue to a dark three room apartment on the ground floor.

She was put on a bedroom window with six panes to each half, and she washed it sitting on the ledge, counting them off one at a time as she went.

Twenty minutes, and the glass came up clean.

Then she did the living room and the venetian blinds, and while she worked the old woman slipped back into the bedroom with a rag.

She came out and said the corners had not been done and two panes had been missed.

Cooke had counted. She had been warned on the corner that morning that this is exactly the move, that they invent a fault at the end so they can shave the pay.

She dropped the rag in the bucket, climbed down off the ledge, told the woman she had washed every pane and that the woman knew it, and walked out leaving the dirty water standing in the middle of the living room floor.

Forty minutes. She was offered payment for the time and turned it down and was back on the corner before eleven.

The second job was the one that broke her.

It was the wet, muggy day after the two day Christmas holiday, and nobody was hiring. She waited with six other women for one hour, then two, and four of them gave up and went home.

A young couple came and looked the line over and picked the woman standing next to her, who was younger and looked fitter, and she went off trailing behind them.

Then a small elderly woman with a bird-like face asked whether she wanted a few hours.

Seventy-five cents an hour, for an amount of work nobody specified.

On the walk to the apartment on Morris Avenue, the woman told her she had been hiring girls off the street for twenty years and had never once been disappointed, because she always picked nice ones.

Then she said Cooke looked like somebody who belonged in an office.

Then she asked her name.

Cooke gave the name Margo, close enough to her own that she would answer to it.

Five minutes later the woman was calling her Margie.

By the end of the day she was calling her Mary.

The apartment was two rooms and a bath with the kitchen at one end of the living room. The woman watched her change into her work clothes, taking stock of her build.

She rinsed clothes and hung them to dry. She dusted down the walls of the whole apartment with a makeshift mop.

She ironed a man's shirt, four full length ruffled curtains and a tablecloth. She took the stove apart and cleaned it through.

She scrubbed the refrigerator, a cabinet, the sink, the tub and the shelves above the sink. She rubbed oil into every piece of furniture in the place.

The old woman sat in a chair the entire time and watched every movement. Once or twice she got up to flick imaginary dust off something Cooke had already finished, and then sat back down.

Last came the floors, which were linoleum, and which were to be done on hands and knees.

Cooke stood up and said she could not do it. She said the method had gone out with the Civil War, that there were easier ways, and that if it had to be done that way there should at least be a knee pad.

The old woman did not raise her voice. She said gently that all her girls did the floors this way, that this was how she liked them done, and that if Mary would just finish this one she would call it a day.

Cooke finished the floor.

Then she changed into her street clothes and the woman counted three dollars and forty cents into her hand, which was exactly what the clock in that apartment said she was owed, and which did not include her carfare.

Twenty cents.

She was too tired to ask for it.

The law had nothing to say about that twenty cents, or about the clock, or about the floor. In 1950, fifteen years after the first exposé, a domestic worker was covered by workmen's compensation only if she put in forty-eight hours a week for one employer, and by unemployment insurance only if she was one of four or more household workers in a single home for fifteen days in the year.

Which is to say she was covered by nothing, because almost nobody worked like that.

The state had free employment offices by then, in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens. They were sited where the demand for household labor was, which meant they were sited where few Black people lived.

There was no household office in Harlem, where most of the applicants came from.

So the women stayed on the corner. And the ones on relief stayed on the corner on purpose, because an employment record would cost them part of a check that was about to be cut again in January.

Here is what it costs to carry this properly, and it costs nothing.

Go and look at Robert McNeill's photographs. The Library of Congress has digitized them with no known restrictions on publication, one of them belongs to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and Fortune magazine would not print a single one of them.

Then find Minnie Marshall's interview, taken on a December day in 1938 and free to read, because she is one of the very few women out of all those corners whose name anybody wrote down.

And when this story comes across your feed with a line about how the mayor stepped in and put a stop to it, add the rest of it. The mayor sent police to collect the women, questioned them about their relief checks, and announced that nothing was wrong.

New York City put up an official marker in 2015 for the colonial slave market that stood at Wall and Pearl Streets from 1711 to 1762. It was the first the city had ever raised for that market, and it arrived more than two hundred and fifty years late.

Then search the marker databases for 167th and Jerome, and search them again for Simpson and Westchester, and see what comes back.

The women who stood there had already worked out the truth of the place long before any of it was written down, and one of them handed it to a stranger on a wet sidewalk in the winter of 1950.

"Don't let them turn the clock back on you."

text:
The trajectory of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from an insurgent working-class outsider to a reliable institutional standard-bearer for the Democratic Party establishment is no longer a matter of quiet debate—it is an explosive schism fracturing the American Left. What was once heralded by progressives as a historic socialist breakthrough inside the halls of capital has metastasized into what critics across the independent left are increasingly branding the "Kamala-fication" of AOC: a calculated retreat into obfuscation, liberal managerial rhetoric, and defensive loyalty to the ruling-class political machine.

As the 2026 midterms approach and early positioning for the 2028 Democratic presidential primary accelerates, the ideological chasm between genuine socialist, anti-imperialist, and anti-capitalist politics and AOC’s brand of electoral reformism has reached a point of open civil war. For a movement built on class struggle, the fundamental question is no longer how to get leftists into high office, but whether high office inevitably absorbs and neutralizes those who enter it.

Fumbling the Easiest Question: The Netanyahu Evasion
The most glaring evidence of this ongoing ideological pivot emerged when Ocasio-Cortez was directly confronted with a straightforward question regarding international law and state violence: Should Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu be arrested by U.S. authorities under International Criminal Court (ICC) warrants upon entering the United States?

For an anti-imperialist movement witnessing a live-streamed genocide in Gaza, the answer is elementary. Yet, rather than offering an unequivocal stance grounded in international law, anti-Zionism, and basic human rights, AOC delivered a convoluted, highly evasive response that left anti-war organizers and working-class supporters stunned. Her hesitation immediately caught the attention of major news outlets across the media landscape, with platforms such as USA Today, The Hill, and The Economic Times pointing out how her hedging underscored the profound structural contradictions of operating within the Democratic Party apparatus.

The public reaction across social media and independent leftist channels was swift, severe, and unforgiving:

"AOC unable to answer a simple question about whether she thinks Netanyahu ahould be arrested when he comes to the US next week. Looks like she's taking word salad lessons from Kamala Harris."— Professor Anthony Zenkus 

"How to screw up the easiest answer in the universe, absolutely pathetic."— Amir 

"Not as bad as when she was asked whether the US should commit ground troops to Taiwan, but pretty bad"— Max Blumenthal 

"She stands for absolutely nothing and is not talented enough to hide it."— Garland Nixon

For principled anti-imperialists, refusing to demand the immediate detention of an indicted war criminal was not a minor public relations blunder or a tactical stumble. It was a clear signal of ideological surrender to the foreign policy consensus of Washington.

Shielding the Establishment: Cover for Hakeem Jeffries
The critique of AOC’s evolution extends far beyond her foreign policy rhetoric; it touches the core of her domestic legislative strategy and her protective posture toward Democratic Party elites. Following revelations that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries—one of the largest congressional recipients of AIPAC campaign funds—had engaged in backchannel, undisclosed meetings with Trump family insider Jared Kushner, progressives expressed deep outrage over the bipartisan fraternization between party bosses and corporate oligarchs.

Yet, when asked to address Jeffries’ meeting, AOC offered a soft chuckle and a mild, deflecting critique regarding Jared Kushner's lack of "transparency," deliberately avoiding any direct accountability or condemnation for Jeffries himself. Media programs like The Young Turks and independent leftist commentators on Due Dissidence highlighted how her reluctance to break ranks with top House leadership reveals a politician who systematically prioritizes access and party standing over anti-capitalist principles.

As political commentator Zaid Jilani observed regarding her communication style:

"She has a Kamala Harris-like habit of saying way too much without saying much at all"— Zaid Jilani

By providing political cover for figures like Jeffries, AOC has increasingly alienated radical organizers, movement builders, and rank-and-file workers who recognize that the Democratic leadership acts as an active barrier to working-class liberation and anti-imperialist solidarity.

The DSA Civil War and the Limits of Electoralism
This rightward drift is not taking place in an isolated vacuum—it is fueling a fierce structural confrontation within the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). As detailed in recent reporting by Axios, the national DSA published its "Workers Deserve More" platform, laying out an explicit vision that included structural and anti-imperialist planks such as defunding the Department of Defense, abolishing the U.S. Senate, and advancing toward the complete abolition of the police and prison industrial complex.

INTELBRIEF: Eritrea’s Quiet Role in Sudan’s Chemical Weapons Scandal

As evidence mounted that Sudan’s military had developed and used chlorine-based chemical weapons against its rivals, Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan made a quiet trip to this tightly controlled capital on the Red Sea. It was his second visit to meet President Isaias Afwerki in less than two months. The second meeting took place on Sept. 4, one day before major American newspapers published a detailed dossier documenting the Sudanese program.
The timing has drawn new scrutiny to a relationship that has largely operated in the shadows: Eritrea’s role as a political and logistical backer of the Sudanese Armed Forces at a moment when those forces faced international accusations of chemical warfare.
On Sept. 5, The Washington Post and The New York Times published internal Sudanese military materials.. documents, videos, intercepted messages and photographs — describing a 2024 effort to produce chlorine munitions. According to the files, a senior officer, Brig. Gen. Tariq Hussain, also known as Tariq Madani, oversaw the design and production of bombs that combined an explosive warhead with roughly 15 kilograms of chlorine gas. The weapons were tested from Merowe Air Base in northern Sudan. 
#Eritrea’s connection to the Sudanese military does not appear in the core of that dossier. Yet a separate body of reporting and evidence shows that Asmara has provided sustained support to the Sudanese army throughout the civil war. Eritrea has hosted training for forces aligned with the Sudanese military, offered political cover, and facilitated a logistics corridor into eastern Sudan and Port Sudan. Analysts tracking aircraft movements have identified #Massawa, Eritrea’s principal Red Sea port and airport, as a recurring transit point for cargo flights linked to Sudanese supply lines. Satellite imagery and flight data have shown #Belarusian Il-76 freighters and other cargo aircraft operating through Massawa in periods of heightened Sudanese military need.
This pattern is not new. A 2017 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea documented a large consignment of blank-firing pistols that docked at Massawa. The Sudanese owner told investigators he preferred the Eritrean port because it was cheaper and administratively simpler to move goods overland into Sudan than to use Port Sudan itself. The United Nations confirmed the Massawa stop through shipping records, establishing a precedent for the route.
The frequency of General Burhan’s recent visits has added weight to questions about the relationship. Eritrean state media described the July 17 and Sept. 4 meetings as part of an ongoing “consultative framework” between the two governments. Neither side has released a detailed account of what was discussed. The second visit, however, occurred on the eve of the publication of the most extensive public evidence yet of Sudan’s chemical weapons effort.
An Arabic-language investigation by Erem News, citing unnamed Sudanese sources, has gone further. It alleged that shipments arriving in Massawa during the war were moved overland into territory controlled by the Sudanese army and that one of General Burhan’s trips to Asmara involved matters connected to the handling or concealment of material related to the prohibited-weapons file. 
 Eritrea’s political and logistical support for the Sudanese Armed Forces is documented across multiple independent sources. What is more gravious is that if Eritrean territory was used to move chlorine stocks, finished chemical munitions, or evidence of the program as per leaked information. 
The combination of a verified chemical weapons uss by SAF a documented supply relationship with Eritrea, a historic arms-transit route through Massawa, and high-level meetings timed with the program’s exposure has created a pattern that investigators say warrants closer examination.

text:
"The deeper problem is that public policy offers no opportunity to run both scenarios and compare the results. We cannot spend six months pursuing a trade war, inspect the damage, and then return to August to conclude the agreement with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

Decisions build on one another. New tariffs create new disputes. Governments acquire political commitments that make compromise harder. Terms that seemed unacceptable before the latest confrontation may become attractive just as the other side loses interest in offering them.

The economy moves on as well. A manufacturer that places its next investment in the U.S. may not reconsider because Ottawa and Washington eventually reconcile. A Canadian supplier that loses a customer may struggle to win it back. Workers and businesses can suffer permanent losses during what politicians describe as temporary bargaining pressure. Waiting is itself a consequential choice.

There’s little appetite for this discussion right now. Canadians are rightly angry. Arguments about economic asymmetry can sound defeatist when people want their government to stand up for them. Yet protecting Canadians requires a dispassionate assessment of what’s realistic and what’s ultimately in the country’s interests.

Some months from now, there’s a good chance that the public debate will change. The question may become what Canada’s economy would have looked like had Ottawa concluded the proposed agreement with Greer.

We’ll never be able to answer precisely. There will be no parallel scenario in which the deal was signed, investment proceeded, and the next round of tariffs never arrived. That uncertainty should admittedly make us careful about claiming what the agreement would have delivered. But it should also make us careful about discarding it."

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

In 2007, Switzerland accidentally invaded Liechtenstein with an armed force of 170 infantry soldiers, and Liechtenstein was completely unaware it had been invaded until the Swiss government called to apologize!

​During a night-time training exercise in bad weather, a company of Swiss soldiers took a wrong turn and marched over 1 mile across the unmarked, open border into the tiny Alpine principality. Because Liechtenstein has no standing military (it abolished its army in 1868) and shares an open border agreement with Switzerland, no border guards or residents noticed the armed troops walking down their roads.

Once the Swiss commander realized his navigational error, the unit sheepishly turned around and marched back into Switzerland. A spokesperson for Liechtenstein's interior ministry brushed off the incident, noting, "It's not like they stormed over here with attack helicopters." 

​Amusingly, this was not an isolated incident, Switzerland has accidentally crossed into or shelled Liechtenstein by mistake several times over the decades, including a 1968 incident where Swiss artillery shells misfired across the border and accidentally hit a Liechtenstein ski resort.  Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾

​Key Historical & Diplomatic Highlights:

A. ​The 1866 Army of 80 That Returned with 81: During the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, Liechtenstein sent an army of 80 soldiers to guard an Alpine pass. They saw zero combat and returned home with 81 men after making a friend, an Austrian military liaison officer, along the way.

B. You Could Once Rent the Entire Country on Airbnb: In 2011, Liechtenstein partnered with a marketing agency to list the entire nation on Airbnb for $70,000 a night. Renters were offered custom street signs, temporary legal tender, a wine-tasting session with the Reigning Prince Hans-Adam II, and a symbolic key to the country.  

C. ​World Leader in Dental Prosthetics: Despite having a population of under 40,000, Liechtenstein is the world's leading manufacturer of false teeth. A single Liechtenstein-based company, Ivoclar Vivadent, produces over 60 million sets of prosthetic teeth every year. 

​SUMMARILY! 
​Liechtenstein's microscopic size, peaceful disposition, and open borders with Switzerland have made it the subject of some of Europe's most unique diplomatic anecdotes, proving that a country doesn't need an army to maintain its sovereignty and humor.

text:
Specificity Is the Unfair Advantage
Most first offers fail for a boring reason.
They’re too broad.
“I help people make money online.”
“I teach mindset.”
“I help entrepreneurs grow.”
“I create content about success.”
That sounds big.
It also gives the reader no reason to believe you are talking to them.
I used to think going wide was the smart move. More people. More reach. More chances. As a former cop and Army veteran building from $0, I learned the opposite:
The narrower the offer, the easier it is to finish, explain, and sell.
Broad Feels Safe. Specific Gets Bought.
Broad offers feel safe because they don’t exclude anyone.
That’s the problem.
When someone lands on a vague offer, they have to do extra work:
•  Is this for me?
•  What exactly do I get?
•  Has this person solved my version of the problem?
Most people won’t do that work. They scroll.
A specific offer removes the guesswork.
Not “I help people build passive income.”
Better: “I help veterans turn one skill they already have into a simple digital product.”
Not “I teach discipline.”
Better: “A 14-day structure for people who can grind at work but can’t stay consistent on their own business.”
The second version is smaller on paper.
It’s bigger in conversion.
Why Specific Offers Are Easier to Build
This is the part people miss.
A vague product is hard to write because you don’t know where to stop.
A specific product has edges.
If you know:
•  who it’s for
•  what problem it removes
•  what result they should have after using it
…then the content of the offer almost writes itself.
You stop adding extra modules “just in case.”
You stop trying to sound impressive.
You start making something usable.
That’s why specificity is not just a marketing trick.
It’s a completion tool.

text:
“Competitive Narratives: Tale of Three Witnesses”

Luke 23:46: Jesus dies on the cross

Text: “Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit.” And having said this, he breathed his last. Luke presents a clear, unambiguous physical death on the cross itself. No rescue. No delay. No alternative cause. Jesus dies directly after speaking.

Key features in Luke: Jesus is conscious and vocal. He voluntarily “commits” his spirit. Death is immediate. No mention of poison, vinegar, or rescue.

Luke’s narrative is simple, clean, and final. Luke shows obedience. In Luke, Jesus commits His spirit into the Father’s hands. It is a picture of surrender, not defeat, but trust. There are days when obedience feels like loss, days when surrender feels like the end. Luke reminds us that obedience is never wasted.

John 19:29–30: Jesus dies after drinking the sour wine

Text: They put a sponge full of sour wine on hyssop and lifted it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished,” and bowed his head and gave up his spirit. John’s sequence is different and introduces a new element: Jesus drinks a substance immediately before dying. John shows fulfillment. In John, Jesus receives the sour wine and declares, “It is finished.” This is the Christ who completes His assignment. There are seasons when G-d calls us to finish what we started, even when it hurts, even when it costs us something. John reminds us that fulfillment is part of faith.

Hebrews 5:7: G-d saved Jesus from death

Text: “In the days of his flesh, he offered up prayers… to the One able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.” Hebrews states plainly. Hebrews shows deliverance. Hebrews tells us Jesus prayed to be saved from death, and He was heard. This is the Christ who overcomes. The Anointed One who is rescued. The Anointed One who is delivered. There are moments when G-d does not ask us to endure, He steps in and saves. Hebrews reminds us that deliverance is real.

This creates two contradictions: Firstly, Contradiction in the cause of death, Luke: Jesus dies after speaking, no external cause, John: Jesus dies after ingesting a substance.

The Greek word for “sour wine” (oxos) is the same substance Roman soldiers used as: a cheap drink, a pain numbing agent, or, in some historical cases, a poisonous or stupefying mixture.

John’s sequence implies: Drink → Statement → Death.

Luke’s sequence implies: Statement → Death.

These cannot be harmonized without forcing the text. 

Secondly, Contradiction in the timing of death; Luke: Jesus dies immediately after speaking.

John: Jesus dies immediately after drinking. Two different triggers. Two different narrative structures. Two different theological agendas.

And Finally, Hebrews 5:7: G-d saved Jesus from death

Text: “In the days of his flesh, he offered up prayers… to the One able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.” Hebrews states plainly: G-d heard Jesus’ prayer and saved him from death.

This directly contradicts both Luke and John. The contradiction with Luke: Luke: Jesus dies on the cross. Hebrews: G-d saved him from death. Both cannot be true simultaneously.

Contradiction with John: John: Jesus dies after drinking the sour wine. Hebrews: Jesus was saved from death. Again, they are mutually exclusive.

:Hebrews’ theological implication: Hebrews presents Jesus as: suffering, praying to be delivered, and successfully delivered. This is not a resurrection text. It is a pre death deliverance (Salvation/Restoration) text. Hebrews does not describe Jesus dying and rising. It describes Jesus not dying because G-d intervened. This is the strongest contradiction of all.

Narrative Implications:

Luke and John contradict each other

They disagree on: the trigger of death, the sequence of events, the physical cause, and the theological meaning. Hebrews contradicts both Luke and John

Hebrews presents a Jesus who: prays to avoid death, is heard, and is saved. This cannot coexist with: Luke’s “he breathed his last,” or John’s “he gave up his spirit.” The early Christ movement had multiple competing narratives; The contradictions reveal: Different communities, Different theological agendas, Different portrayals of Jesus’ end.

The Synoptic tradition (Luke) vs. The Johannine tradition (John) vs. The early high priestly theology (Hebrews). These are not the same story. The contradiction between the witnesses is not a problem, it is a revelation. Luke teaches us to obey. John teaches us to finish. Hebrews teaches us to overcome.

And in our own walk: Some days feel like Luke — surrender. Some days feel like John   completion. Some days feel like Hebrews — rescue. Our lives has the same three seasons: A Luke season where G-d asks you to surrender. A John season where G-d asks you to finish. A Hebrews season where G-d steps in and saves. Jesus meets us in all three.

Daily Challenge

Identify which witness speaks to your life today: Luke, Is G-d asking you to, surrender something? John, Is G-d asking you to finish something? Hebrews, Is God preparing to deliver you from something? Write it down. Pray over it, walk in it.

Forgiven Temple Ministries 
“Worship Without Walls”
 — Pastor Mark

text:
Zelda: OoT Rebirth – The Illusion

I was 15 in 1998, when Ocarina of Time came out. The first time I saw the TV commercial, I literally stopped breathing from the first frame to the last. From that moment on, I had only one goal in life: to play that game. I didn’t have a N64, and I had no savings to buy one. I still wonder how I managed it, but after mortgaging every Christmas and birthday present with my relatives, a week later I had it.

What followed were the two most beautiful months of my childhood, which ended at the exact moment the credits appeared. I already knew that nothing would ever be the same, that I would never again be amazed to that degree. Even today, I look at my old N64 cartridge and tell myself that the child I was is still locked inside it, exploring Hyrule Field for eternity.

That’s how much I was waiting for this remake. But from what I saw today, this game will not be Ocarina of Time. It will be its ghost, a distant cousin, nothing more. It couldn’t be. The only way would have been to make an entirely new Zelda. A remake alone cannot bring it back to life.

It’s beautiful. It’s well animated. You want to believe. But beneath the lighting, the cutscenes and the reorchestrations, a gaping crack shatters the illusion. A new costume on an old man does not make him young again : he remains an old man. Ocarina of Time’s youth was never dependent on its graphics. That was an illusion we all wanted to cling to, myself first. Makeup never completely hides the wrinkles. And those wrinkles are likely to be painfully visible once the controller is in hand.

You cannot truly understand a game without having known it in the context of its time, and Ocarina of Time is probably the most emblematic example of that idea. At launch, it was the first 3D Zelda, the first transposition of its puzzle logic and quests into a volumetric space. Everything had to be invented, discovered, understood. That is precisely what made it the legend it is today. Yes, it had some of the most beautiful music the series has ever had. Yes, its world felt enormous. Yes, its atmospheres were unlike anything seen before. But that was at the time.

Its legend rests on the perfect conjunction of a narrative, a structure and an art direction that were implacable for 1998, and the novelty of a gameplay born from a technology still taking its first steps. Its flawless execution on both fronts is what made it what it is.

In 1998 there was no internet to hand you the solution the moment you were stuck on a puzzle. At best, you bought a paper guide. I spent weeks locked in the Forest Temple, going in circles, because my mind, still learning to think in 3D, kept missing elements that seem completely obvious today. A temple in Zelda had a different meaning then, a different aura. You knew when you entered; you never knew when you would come out. I wandered for hours and days through that world solving quests whose logic, now the most ordinary of all, completely escaped me. That mystery, that thinking you had to construct, those challenges born from discovering a 3D logic materialized for the first time: that is Ocarina of Time. 

You can recreate an atmosphere, add textures and rendering effects, make animations more dynamic, stage spectacular cutscenes. But what lies underneath, the game’s own soul, that shiver when you enter a temple without knowing when you will leave it, and the indescribable satisfaction when you finally do, how do you recreate that? Because contrary to what many imagine, that is Ocarina of Time. And this remake will not recreate it.

How long will the graphical wow last once the controller is in hand? Thirty minutes? An hour at most? And then? What happens when the wrapping is no longer enough and the only thing left visible is static, outdated gameplay logic that everyone already knows by heart? What feeling will take hold of players at that moment?

When you have seen NPCs running at full speed toward their houses to take shelter from the rain in Breath of the Wild, what sensation can you feel in front of a motionless NPC who has no life outside his line of dialogue? What soul can a village still have after you have seen children run to school at dawn and leave at four o’clock, when you find yourself facing inhabitants trapped in an infinite loop who exist only by day or by night? What can the people of Ocarina of Time still generate today?

That vast field that made you dream the moment you turned the console on, thirty years ago : what sense of elsewhere can it still offer? When you have tamed wild horses and fought at full gallop against enemy mounts with sword and arrows, what can gentle Epona still provide by merely jumping over a low wall? Yes, there are thousands of blades of grass, flares and impressive atmospheric effects. How long will they sustain the illusion that there is nothing else?

That cute pond and its twenty fish : what will they generate for players who have fished every river and pond for more than ten years and cooked the catch?The magic of Ocarina of Time was bound to its era. To bring it back to life, you would have had to bring back to life what formed its essence : the newness of everything you could do in it. The illusion of novelty through technique will not make it new. It will do the opposite.

That feeling of absolute freedom and discovery has already been recreated. It is called Breath of the Wild. That is the closest thing to an Ocarina of Time remake we could have hoped for, and the most effective one. This Rebirth version will not bring anything back to life. You would need a time machine, and you would have to forget every evolution that Zelda gameplay, and every 3D game that followed from it, has brought over thirty years. It could not be accomplished, and it will not be. 

Good for those who will find a source of nostalgia in it. But the seams are likely to split along the way.

Ocarina of Time is dead. Long live Ocarina of Time. May it rest in peace.
