text:
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty

1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.” 

Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.

Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.

This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.

Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.

Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.

Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America. 

No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.

Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.

Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.

Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017. 

In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.

Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.

What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.

He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.

No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.

Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.

That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.

He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.

The authorities is speaking of your neighbor and his liberty. 

Even though the beginning of this chapter describes Peter’s audience as “disallowed of men” (as in cast out from their civil societies), “lively stones” in a “spiritual house” as a “holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (as opposed to hewn stones in a carnal, worldlyjurisdiction, as civil slaves, who give up forcedsacrifices through taxation), a “chosen generation” (as in a nation of one kind of people), a “royal priesthood, an holy nation” (as in a kingdom of priests, freed from former civil slavery), “a peculiar people” (which will be examined shortly) who have been called out “of darkness into his marvellous light” (left the civil jurisdictions of the world to enter the Kingdom of God), those contentious against the Gospelof God still use this passage to legitimize going under the power of human civil government.
To coincide with the notion of being “a peculiar people,” Peter also describes his audience as being “strangers and pilgrims” in verse eleven. This idea of God’s people being “in the world, but not of the world” is one that encompasses both testaments, as we have already touched on in the previous blog post:
“To further compound this point, in Daniel 2:25, he is referred to as a ‘captive’ or ‘exile’ of Judah. Often throughout scripture, this concept is coupled with the word ‘stranger’ which sometimes means ‘resident’ or ‘alien‘ as opposed to ‘citizen’ and sometimes means ‘without a share,’ as in possesses no entitlement to the strange nation’s provision.”
It is this same sort of provision and entitlementthat Peter recalls with the phrase “fleshly lustswhich war against the soul,” because socialist provision from Benefactors who exercise authority brings one into civil bondage. If you abstain from taking government benefits your soul will have peace, because you will be free from bondage, under God’s jurisdiction and eligible for his Providence instead. It is because Christians belong to a separate civil society with its own laws, customs, system of welfareand method of organization that it even becomes relevant to instruct them to have their “conversation honest among the Gentiles.”
The word Gentiles comes from the greek “ethnos,” referring to “a race” or “nation,” as people joined by practicing similar customs or common culture.” Compared to God’s people, anybody belonging to another god in another civil society separate from their own, would be considered a gentile. The world of Rome, under which the early Christians were not subject citizens, was a gentile nation. The word for “conversation” in the same verse is from the Greek word “anastrephó” which simply means “conduct” or “behavior,” but is curiously translated “turn upside down” when described of the early Christians in Acts 17:
“But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people. And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also; Whom Jason hath received: and these all do contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus. And they troubled the people and the rulers of the city, when they heard these things. And when they had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go.” (Acts 17:5-9)
This connection helps to reveal just what kind of honest “conversation” that the Christians were having with the Gentiles. Their conduct upset the Roman and Herodian Jews because they were not counted among Roman and Herodian citizenship, and preaching repentance unto citizenship of the Kingdom of God. They were not subject to the decrees of Caesar.
They had another king entirely.

Every new clip changes the forecast, outfit or location on the map, but the presenter stays identical, which makes the entire page feel like one real weather channel instead of a stream of random AI videos.

She posts 7 times a day across TikTok, Instagram and Shorts. Storm alerts. Heat waves. Snow maps. Weekend forecasts. Ten-second clips where she points at Arkansas, Texas, Florida or California while the weather graphic moves behind her. The format is simple enough to produce repeatedly and familiar enough that viewers immediately understand what they're watching.

By month four the page crossed 430,000 followers and several clips passed 3 million views. He turned one AI character into a daily weather channel without a studio, camera crew or real presenter, and the same face appearing in every forecast helped turn casual viewers into repeat viewers.

$6,800 a month came from sponsorships. $5,100 from affiliate offers. $4,200 from subscriptions. Another $2,800 came from digital promotions. Total monthly revenue reached $18,900 while the entire production stack stayed under $240.

Stack that built her: Grok for concepts and the presenter workflow, Flux for reference images, custom LoRA for consistency, Kling for motion, Claude for scripts and n8n for scheduling and automation.

The forecast changes every day.

The presenter doesn't.

text:
Blockbuster didn’t lose to a better movie. It lost to a better habit.
In the early 2000s they had roughly 9,000 stores and nearly 60,000 employees. Friday night meant walking the aisles, hunting a new release, and paying a late fee if you forgot the tape. That model printed money—until a small DVD-by-mail company offered to sell itself for about $50 million. Blockbuster passed.
The miss wasn’t just “they should have bought Netflix.” The miss was refusing to see that customers would eventually pay to avoid the store. Late fees were a feature of their profit, not a bug. Physical inventory, leases, and the assumption that people would keep driving to a strip mall locked them into yesterday’s behavior. By 2010 they were in bankruptcy. One independently owned store in Bend, Oregon is what’s left.
The useful part isn’t the punchline. It’s the pattern: a company can be huge, loved, and still die from protecting the thing that already works instead of the thing customers are quietly starting to prefer. Convenience beat ritual. Subscription beat punishment. The catalog in your living room beat the catalog on the wall.
If you grew up in those stores, you remember the smell of plastic cases and the Saturday-night scramble for the last copy. That memory is real. The lesson is just as real: the moment you start charging people for friction they no longer have to accept, someone else will remove the friction.
What’s the last “this will never change” business you still use out of habit?

text:
Facts Grok;
Mother Teresa (Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, 1910–1997) founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950. The order grew into hundreds of homes worldwide for the dying, lepers, orphans, and destitute. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonized in 2016. The popular image is of a selfless saint. The documented record is more mixed and specific.

Medical care in the homes was basic by design, not modern hospice or hospital standard.  
Robin Fox, then editor of The Lancet, visited the Kalighat Home for Dying Destitutes in 1994. He found decisions often made by sisters and untrained volunteers rather than doctors, diagnoses that were haphazard, and no strong analgesics in the formulary. He praised the cleanliness and kindness but said the approach was distinct from the hospice movement. Multiple volunteers independently described needles rinsed in tap or cold water and reused, aspirin given for terminal cancer pain, and cold-water bathing of patients with respiratory illness. Treatable patients were sometimes mixed with the dying.

Mother Teresa’s own words explain the philosophy. She said it was “very beautiful for the poor to accept their lot, to share it with the passion of Christ” and that “suffering is a gift from God.” She described pain as “the kiss of Jesus.” Defenders note that morphine was scarce even in Calcutta hospitals in that era and that the homes were never intended as hospitals; they took people hospitals had already rejected so they would not die alone on the street. After her death some hygiene and pain-management practices improved.

Donations were large and poorly documented by modern charity standards.  
The order has never published a full global audit. It officially says it does not fundraise and lives on “Divine Providence.” Former sister Susan Shields described sacks of mail containing checks of $50,000 or more and one New York account holding about $50 million in a single year. A 2013 University of Montreal analysis estimated roughly $100 million raised before 1980 with a low percentage visibly spent on the poor. UK filings for the local trust show multi-million-pound annual income and spending, but overall finances remain opaque; money tended to flow upward to central accounts rather than automatically to local upgrades. The sisters themselves lived extremely austerely. The core question is not personal embezzlement but whether the scale of donations should have produced better medical infrastructure.

She accepted money and honors from controversial sources.  
Charles Keating donated more than $1 million and lent his private jet. After his savings-and-loan fraud conviction, Mother Teresa wrote the judge praising his generosity to “God’s poor” and asking for clemency; she did not return the money when prosecutors requested it. In 1980–81 she visited Haiti, received the Legion of Honour from dictator Jean-Claude Duvalier, and publicly praised Michele Duvalier’s familiarity with the poor. The Duvalier regime was a corrupt dictatorship accused of human-rights abuses. Similar pragmatic associations occurred with other strongmen. She treated the money as usable for her work regardless of origin.

Her own medical treatment was more advanced than what patients received.  
She had a pacemaker implanted in Calcutta in 1989. In 1991–92 she was treated at Scripps Clinic in California for pneumonia and heart problems, including angioplasty, and also received care in New York. She took pain medication for her own chronic back and other issues. Critics call this a double standard. Defenders say her continued work required her survival and that she accepted whatever care was offered.

The factual picture is therefore neither pure hagiography nor simple fraud. She built a large, austere religious order that gave basic care and presence to people others ignored. Her theology treated suffering as spiritually valuable, which shaped medical choices that later observers found inadequate.

The image’s claim is inaccurate. California has not approved a bill authorizing the purchase of burned Pacific Palisades lots specifically to convert them into affordable housing. https://t.co/VpnFRpye07

Palisades lies inside the City of Los Angeles, not unincorporated county land. Rebuilding debates now center on density laws, investor purchases, and insurance, not a state land-bank for affordable housing in the Palisades.

text:
No joke — over the past two weeks, I've purchased two portable CD players from eBay for my car. The reason? The digital-to-analog converter (DAC) in so-called "retro" or "vintage" portable CD players is superior to those $40 ones on Amazon (trust me, I tried one already). 

I've been a CD fan for years. In Northern California, we're fortunate to have a number of music stores that sell "used" CDs and other physical media, often for far less than what an album sells for new on iTunes or Amazon Music. Same music, less money — and you can trade them back in for a little bit of store credit.

Nice to see CDs are making a comeback, but I'm not looking forward to the trouble of finding new titles at my local music and thrift stores.

Protip: If, like me, your car lacks a CD player and you're looking to eBay for a portable one, make sure you get a CD player that has a dedicated LINE OUT port, not just a headphone jack! Many mid-1990s models from Sony, Aiwa, Fisher and Panasonic have them. They work so much better when connected via an aux jack in a car compared to a standard headphone port.

Also, look for one that offers the smallest electronic skip protection buffer. Somethign around 10 seconds is plenty for a trip in the car — you want the LOWEST amount of skip protection buffer for the HIGHEST quality music. (The "buffer" pre-loads parts of a song into the CD player's RAM, which involves compression — the longer the ESP, the higher the compression and the lower the quality of music).

Last, if you can find one, the Optimus CD-3400 model — that SPECIFIC model — is an audiophile's dream. You can sometimes score one on eBay for around $100, but they're usually priced much higher. https://t.co/KggCyrRbUV

text:
Barry Morphew, the Colorado man accused of murdering his wife, Suzanne Morphew, is back behind bars after an alleged hit-and-run — and dramatic video captures the moments before he allegedly drove away.

On Aug. 26, Morphew was out on a $3 million bond and under restrictions that generally confined him to his home when authorities say he struck two vehicles in Denver. A witness told police Morphew had been driving “aggressively” before the crashes.

Video recorded by Christina, one of the drivers involved, shows her repeatedly asking Morphew for his license and insurance information. Morphew allegedly said he did not have insurance, tried to rub scratches off her vehicle with his hand and T-shirt and offered her $300 for the damage.

After Christina refused the money and said she was calling police, court documents allege Morphew drove away, nearly hitting another person and going over a curb as he left.

GPS data later showed Morphew had left his home and traveled toward Denver International Airport, where his attorneys said he may have been going to pick up his daughter. Prosecutors argued the trip violated his bond conditions and raised concerns that he could be a flight risk.

A judge subsequently ordered Morphew to remain inside his home at all times with “no exceptions.” He was arrested the following night on a warrant for allegedly failing to comply with his bond conditions.

Morphew has not been charged in connection with the alleged hit-and-run.
He has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the death of Suzanne, who disappeared on Mother’s Day 2020. Her remains were discovered in 2023, and her death was later ruled a homicide.

Watch the encounter that ultimately put Morphew’s freedom in jeopardy.

text:
Colorado already treats hunting as a population-management tool for black bears.

CPW manages bears by individual Data Analysis Units, setting objectives to reduce or stabilize populations and adjusting hunting opportunity accordingly. For 2026, eight of Colorado’s 17 bear DAUs have a population-reduction objective. Some units already offer unlimited over-the-counter opportunities specifically where CPW wants additional harvest. 

The conflict numbers make the larger question about hunting worth proposing.

CPW recorded 3,529 bear incident reports in 2023, 5,031 in 2024 and 5,298 in 2025. Food-related incidents accounted for thousands of those reports. 

Hunting obviously isn’t the entire solution. Securing garbage, removing attractants, drought and natural forage conditions, development in bear habitat and public behavior all matter.

And increasing licenses statewide without regard to local population data would be poor wildlife management.

But where bear populations are healthy, conflict mortality is high and CPW’s objective is already to reduce the population, there is a legitimate question about whether hunters could shoulder more of that management.

A bear harvested in season provides meat, recreation and conservation revenue.

A habituated bear euthanized after repeatedly entering homes is simply dead.

Should Colorado expand targeted bear-hunting opportunity in the areas producing the most conflicts?

text:
Boulder voters will decide in November whether to approve a $400 million bond.

What is actually on the ballot:
→ Repaid over 20 years, it comes to roughly $650 million — more than the city's entire annual budget today.
→ The city has published a list of projects the money would pay for.
→ The ballot measure does not commit the city to building any of them.

Aquiles La Grave, one of six candidates for mayor of Boulder, joined me on @the_bear_roars for the second time. We recorded live in front of an audience at Tulagi Music Festival.

His argument is that Boulder is not short on agreement about what it wants: a downtown that works, homes young families can afford, parks that feel safe.

His own answer is unglamorous. As mayor, nothing would reach the full council agenda without a budget and a named source of revenue behind it.

A property owner with three acres just outside Boulder's city limits offered to bring the land into the city and build six homes for families.

Boulder says it wants more housing. The owner was willing to build it.

The city came back with the costs associated with doing so. The numbers were high enough that the homes could not be sold at a price the market would support.

Nobody did anything wrong. Everybody followed the rules.

I pushed back on plenty of Aquiles' arguments during the conversation, and I have invited Mayor Aaron Brockett to join me on the podcast to make his own case.

A strong Boulder makes the whole Front Range stronger. An argument about how, rather than about what, is progress on its own.

text:
If you need a screen to tell you when to breathe, you have already surrendered your soul.

The modern tragedy is watching high-agency builders outsource basic biological autonomy to consumer gadgets.

When you install an app to tell you when to stand, breathe, or focus, you are not optimizing performance. You are training your nervous system to become an external slave to hardware.

The biological cost of keeping these devices in your physical space is far more destructive than people realize.

Researchers at UT Austin (Ward, Duke, Gneezy, and Bos) published a landmark paper in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research titled "Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One's Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity."

They tested two core pillars of human leverage across hundreds of participants:

Working Memory Capacity (measured via the Automated Operation Span task)

Functional Fluid Intelligence (measured via Raven's Progressive Matrices)

Participants were randomly assigned to three conditions: 
• Desk: Phone placed directly on the desk in plain sight 
• Pocket/Bag: Phone kept in their pocket or personal bag 
• Other Room: Phone left entirely outside the testing environment

The data exposed a brutal reality:
• Proximity destroys cognitive capacity: Participants with their phone on the desk suffered significant drops in both working memory and fluid intelligence compared to those who left their devices in another room.

• Turning it off does not work: In experiment two, researchers instructed half the participants to completely power their phones off. It changed nothing. The cognitive deficit remained identical whether the phone was powered on or completely dead.

• Flipping it face-down is useless: Screen visibility offered no protection. The brain still tracks the device.

• The drain is completely unconscious: Over 85% of participants stated that the phone's location had zero impact on their performance. The modal response to how often they thought about their phone was "not at all."

Your prefrontal cortex burns significant metabolic energy continuously suppressing the automatic impulse to check the device, even when you consciously believe you are 100% focused on your work.

If you are highly dependent on your smartphone, this tax hits you the hardest.

You cannot solve ambient cognitive drainage with discipline, willpower, or "Do Not Disturb" toggles. You must engineer physical friction:

• The 10-Meter Separation Protocol: During your primary 90-minute deep work block, place your phone in an entirely different room behind a closed door. Out of sight inside a pocket is not enough. It must be physically inaccessible.

• Analog Hardware Anchors: Replace smartwatch vibrations and phone alarms with a mechanical desk timer. Analog tools perform a single closed-loop function with zero branching pathways to digital novelty.

• Paper-First Task Architecture: Define your single highest-leverage task on a blank 3x5 index card before opening any monitor. If an objective is not written on physical paper, it does not exist during your morning block.

• Perimeter Defense in the Bedroom: Never charge your phone within arm's reach of your bed. Waking up next to a glass rectangle forces your brain into reactive processing before your feet touch the floor.

Focus is not a software feature delivered over Bluetooth.

It is a sovereign biological asset protected by irreversible environmental architecture.

Kill the alerts. Build the physical wall. Reclaim your operating bandwidth.

Bookmark this architecture. Follow for systems on focus and cognitive sovereignty.

text:
Appalachia is a bit of a double-edged sword. Sure, it's predominantly White, mostly Irish. The problem there is that there are not many jobs, and drug and alcohol abuse is very high. However, the violent crime rate there is half the national average. Many parts of Appalachia are fairly isolated, so there's no big source of employment. There aren't any factories or large employers that most of these people could drive to, walk to, or ride a bike to. As a consequence, many are on welfare. And the local schools don't have the biggest budgets, as you can imagine. 

My grandfather told me a story about people from Appalachia that used to come across one or two states to come and work for him. Back then, my grandfather was still managing the generational family farm, not a small farm by most standards, thousands of acres. Some people from Appalachia came and worked for him at the farm. 

He also ran a foundry at the time. There were periods where they were so hard up for labor that they would offer to buy clothes, shoes, and boots for new workers. That would entice people to come from hundreds of miles away, including Appalachia, to work at the foundry. 

In modern pop culture there were a couple of episodes, I believe from PBS -  a two-part documentary on a guy from Appalachia named Jesco White. He was an Elvis impersonator, a tap dancer, and a horrible drunk, and those scenes in the documentary will give you an idea of what it's like in Appalachia.

An analog to Eastern Europe and Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, etc. Just think of people in these small provincial villages who drink a lot. Quite similar to Appalachia.

text:
Dino Mavrookas: The Man With a Vision to Rebuild American Shipbuilding
@MavrookasD
What does ancient Greek history have to do with the name of his company, Saronic?
His company went from promising startup to a household name in defense circles in the summer of 2026. In June, a 24-foot Corsair unmanned surface vessel operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59 pulled two U.S. Army Apache pilots from the water off Oman after their helicopter was downed near the Strait of Hormuz — the first publicly known SAR personnel recovery by an American uncrewed boat.
A month later, three Corsairs were used as one-way attack drones against Iran’s Bandar Abbas Naval Base, striking a submarine and ship-maintenance facility. It was the first combat use of sea drones by U.S. forces.

Those two missions — rescue and strike, both in the same contested Gulf waters — put Saronic on the map.

Dino Mavrookas, a former Navy SEAL now betting billions on rebuilding American shipbuilding, sat down with Molly O’Shea for Part II of her inside look at the company. The conversation is blunt:
China built more than 1,000 commercial ships last year. The United States built five.
China holds 57% of global shipbuilding capacity.

The U.S. Navy sits at roughly 290 ships. Congress set a 355-ship minimum in 2018. The service now says it needs 381 manned hulls just to start — an unreachable target if America keeps thinking in the conditions of the past.
Autonomy, private capital, and a new generation of defense primes are the bet.

How was the name “Saronic” chosen?

The name almost didn’t happen. Mavrookas and his wife Georgia, both Greek, were reading about the Battle of Salamis, when the united Greek navies defeated a much larger Persian fleet. He floated “Salamis.” She pushed back and offered “Saronic” instead — after the gulf where the outnumbered Greeks wrecked a superior fleet. He didn’t like it at first. Three days later, it stuck.

In 480 BC, a smaller, faster Greek fleet lured a far larger and more lavish Persian armada into the narrow waters between the island of Salamis and Athens, in the Saronic Gulf, and won. Not with bigger ships. Not with more gold. With agility, numbers where it counted, and the will to fight on their own terms. Ancient Greek naval history inspired the company’s name.

The parallel is the entire thesis: you don’t win naval power by building the most exquisite, most expensive ships. You win by building the ones that can actually show up, in volume, and change the geometry of the fight.

That’s the story Dino tells in the interview — from the atrophy of American yards, to Port Alpha’s $3 billion bet in Brownsville, to why he thinks five to ten new defense primes will emerge this decade, and why the next decade of American shipbuilding will be decided by people more than by capital.

The full conversation is here: Molly O’Shea’s post @MollySOShea
The name origin lands around the 25-minute mark.

Worth the watch if you care about the Navy, modern naval warfare, shipbuilding, and more.

The vehicle has been identified as the Dive-LD, an autonomous underwater vehicle developed by Anduril. The platform is designed for extended underwater missions, with an endurance of up to 10 days and an operating depth of up to 6,000 meters.

Its modular architecture allows it to be configured for a range of missions, including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, mine warfare, seafloor mapping, seabed operations and precision payload deployment. The Dive-LD reportedly offers more than 1 cubic metre of payload capacity and can be deployed from piers and various vessels.

text:
Tulane Green Wave

The Return of Kam Hamilton 

Kam Hamilton is an immediate veteran upgrade for a Tulane D-line that lost its entire 2025 CFP starting front. The 6-4, 292-pound Zachary product just returned as a fifth-year player after going undrafted and is already in the rotation. 

Eligibility was confirmed about an hour before kickoff.

The eligibility path
Hamilton never redshirted. He graduated in May 2026 after four seasons and was auto-enrolled in the 2026 NFL Draft. He worked out with the Saints and Cardinals but did not sign. 

A new NCAA five-year eligibility rule did not grandfather the 2022 class, so he needed the injunction. 

The American Conference also stated that NFL tryouts would not trigger a penalty. Tulane will not be punished if the ruling is later overturned. 

Tulane was the only FBS school that offered him out of Zachary High, where he started on the offensive line for the 15-0 2021 LHSAA 5A state champions before switching to defense.

Production and traits
Career totals through 2025 (54 games, 22-23 starts):
•  90 tackles
•  12 sacks
•  16.5 tackles for loss
•  3 forced fumbles
•  3 passes defended

Year-by-year:
•  2022 (FR): 15 tackles, 0.5 sacks
•  2023 (SO): 25 tackles, 4 sacks, 6 TFL, 1 FF
•  2024 (JR): 21 tackles, 4.5 sacks, 6 TFL, 2 FF, 9 starts, third-team All-AAC
•  2025 (SR): 29 tackles, 3 sacks, 4 TFL, 3 PD, 13 starts

He is listed as a DE but he can play inside or outside. Strength and awareness are his calling cards; he occupies blockers and still produces sacks and TFLs from the interior.
 
What the 2026 D-line needed:
The 2025 starting four from the Ole Miss CFP game are gone: Hamilton was expected to be with the Saints, Harvey Dyson transferred to NC State, Santana Hopper to Colorado, and Tre’Von McAlpine to Kansas. Preseason pieces were transfers Derrick Shepard Jr. (NT, experienced after a 2025 UAB-to-Tulane move) and Ed Smith IV (DT from South Alabama) plus a young rotation (Josh Lewis, Reshad Sterling, Geordan Guidry, Armondous Cooley, Jordyn Crites, PaLanding Drammeh). 
The room was described as talented and deep but inexperienced. They rotate heavily. Duke exposed the run defense (250 rushing yards, Nate Sheppard 227). 

What he specifically adds
•  Experience and leadership in a young room under new DL coach Eric McDaniel. Shepard and Smith IV were the main veterans; Hamilton is the guy with the most Tulane snaps and starts.
•  Interior run-stopping presence. Size and strength to occupy double teams so linebackers (Dickson Agu, Chris Rodgers, Makai Williams) and the bandit (Jah’rie Garner) can flow. This was the biggest Week 1 need.
•  Pass-rush from inside. Consistent 3-4.5 sack seasons give the front another interior threat instead of relying only on edges.
•  Scheme versatility in Tulane’s 4-2-5 / multiple looks under DC Tayler Polk and co-DC Nate Fuqua. He can two-gap or one-gap depending on alignment.
•  Culture and motivation. Local product who overcame a hearing impairment, just missed the NFL, and is playing for a fifth year on an injunction. Will Hall’s comment after the Duke game: “I think he can help us a lot.” 

He is not a flashy edge rusher who will post 10-sack seasons. He is a high-floor, high-motor 292-pound interior piece who knows the program, already knows the calls, and immediately improves the rotation quality on a front that needed exactly that after the 2025 attrition. Expect him to stay in the two-deep mix at DT for the rest of the season.

Explain how. 

The two-state solution remains the official international formula, yet its viability looks weaker than the rhetoric suggests.Palestinian leadership rejected partition or statehood offers in 1937 (Peel), 1947 (UN Partition Plan), after 1967 (Khartoum “Three Noes”), at Camp David 2000 (Barak/Clinton parameters covering 91-95% of the West Bank + Gaza + land swaps), and in 2008 (Olmert offer of ~93-97% of the West Bank with swaps, a Gaza corridor, and limited refugee numbers). Arafat walked away from Camp David without a counter-offer; Abbas did not accept Olmert’s map. Critics of those offers say they still left Israel controlling settlement blocs, water and security arrangements that would have produced a fragmented entity. Both readings have evidence.Israel’s 2005 Gaza disengagement is the closest real-world test of withdrawal. All 21 settlements and the military left. Hamas then won the 2006 legislative election (44% of the vote, 74 seats under the mixed system), seized Gaza from Fatah in 2007, and turned the territory into a launch pad. Rocket fire, which predated the pull-out, increased in range. Israel imposed a blockade. Multiple wars followed. Some data show fewer Israeli deaths from Gaza in the first years after 2005 than during the Second Intifada, but October 2023 erased any residual security argument in Israeli public opinion.Hamas’s 1988 charter called for Israel’s destruction. The 2017 document dropped the most explicit antisemitic language and treated a state on the 1967 lines as a “national consensus” formula, while still rejecting recognition of Israel and keeping the claim to all of historic Palestine.

text:
Bitcoin fund flows show investors trading Fed rate path, not exiting market: CoinShares

Bitcoin fund flows show investors trading the Fed rate path, not exiting the market, according to the latest data from CoinShares. Digital asset investment products saw another week of outflows, but the numbers tell a more nuanced story than a simple bearish retreat. The market is repositioning for a potential September rate hike, a shift that is keeping Bitcoin pinned below the psychologically critical $80,000 mark.

Investors are not fleeing the asset class; rather, they are adjusting exposure to reflect a changing macro reality. The outflows are concentrated in short-term trading products, while longer-term holders appear to be staying put. This suggests a market that is actively trading monetary policy expectations rather than one experiencing a crisis of confidence.

WHAT HAPPENED

According to the latest CoinShares report, Bitcoin funds recorded modest outflows last week, continuing a trend seen over the past month. The report highlights that trading volumes spiked significantly, indicating that the movement was driven by active positioning rather than passive liquidation.

The core driver is the shifting odds on Federal Reserve policy. Markets are now pricing in a growing probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the September meeting, a stark reversal from earlier in the summer when cuts were expected. This repricing has pushed yields higher and strengthened the US dollar, creating headwinds for risk assets like Bitcoin.

CoinShares analysts note that the outflows are primarily from products that offer leveraged or short-term exposure. Data suggests that while the total assets under management dipped, the volume of shares outstanding for long-term holding vehicles remained relatively stable. This divergence is a clear signal that the selling pressure is coming from traders adjusting to the macro calendar, not from investors abandoning the asset.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR CRYPTO

The crypto market has spent the last two years trading in lockstep with liquidity expectations. When the Fed signals easing, Bitcoin rallies; when it tightens, Bitcoin corrects. The current situation is a textbook example of this dynamic. Bitcoin’s struggle to break $80,000 is not a failure of the asset itself, but a reflection of the monetary environment it operates in.

A rate hike in September would tighten financial conditions at a time when the crypto market is already dealing with reduced speculative interest. However, the data from CoinShares suggests that the "strong hands" are not selling. The outflows are relatively small compared to the total market cap, and they are being absorbed without panic.

This resilience matters. It implies that the institutional bid for Bitcoin remains intact, even as short-term traders reduce risk. The market is essentially building a base for the next leg of the rally, waiting for the Fed to signal an end to its tightening cycle. For crypto investors, the key takeaway is that macro data, particularly CPI prints and jobless claims, will likely have a more significant impact on price action than isolated crypto-specific news.

WHAT TRADERS SHOULD WATCH

For traders looking at the next few weeks, the focus should be on the Fed speakers and the economic calendar. The CFTC positioning data will also be crucial to monitor, as it will confirm whether the leveraged community is continuing to shed risk or if shorts are becoming overcrowded.

The immediate resistance level remains the $80,000 mark. A daily close above this level on high volume would likely trigger a short squeeze, as many traders have placed stop-losses just above this psychological barrier. Conversely, a break below the recent support at $75,000 could open the door to a deeper correction toward the $70,000 range.

Pay close attention to the 10-year Treasury yield. If yields continue to spike, Bitcoin will likely face continued selling pressure. However, if yields stabilize or reverse course, the path of least resistance for BTC will tilt upward. Traders should also watch the options market for the September expiry; a large concentration of open interest at the $80,000 strike suggests that market makers may be actively capping the price to hedge their books.

MARKET SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

The current sentiment is best described as NEUTRAL, aligning with the data presented in the fund flows. The market is not in a state of euphoria, nor is it in a state of capitulation. Instead, it is in a holding pattern, waiting for a macro catalyst to provide direction.

Indicators supporting this view include the relatively low volatility compared to historical averages, the stability of long-term holder supply, and the fact that funding rates on major exchanges are hovering near zero. This suggests that the leverage has been flushed out of the system, creating a healthier foundation for the next move.

In the short term, expect continued chop until the Fed decision. In the medium to long term, the outlook remains constructive. Inflation is still cooling on a year-over-year basis, and the labor market is showing signs of softening, which historically precedes a dovish pivot. The current rate hike expectations might be a "hawkish trap," and if the Fed disappoints the hawks in September, Bitcoin could see a violent rally to new highs. Traders should prepare for volatility but remain patient with their core positions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Bitcoin failing to break $80,000?
The primary resistance is coming from macroeconomic factors. Markets are pricing in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in September, which strengthens the US dollar and pushes bond yields higher. This creates a headwind for risk assets like Bitcoin, as investors can get a better risk-free return in traditional markets. The fund flows show that traders are reducing exposure to adjust for this, rather than exiting the market entirely.

Are the outflows from Bitcoin funds a bearish signal?
Not necessarily. The data from CoinShares indicates the outflows are concentrated in short-term and leveraged products, suggesting active trading rather than a broad exit. Long-term holders appear to be maintaining their positions. This implies a neutral to cautiously optimistic outlook, where investors are waiting for clarity on the Fed's path before adding to their exposure.

What will be the next major catalyst for Bitcoin's price?
The next significant catalyst will be the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision in September, along with the accompanying economic projections. Additionally, the release of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data just before that meeting will be crucial. If inflation comes in cooler than expected, it could force the Fed to pause, which would likely ignite a rally in Bitcoin and other risk assets.

text:
She sent out 2,800 résumés. Fewer than twenty interviews. Zero offers.
Zhou Jinniya, a master’s graduate in broadcasting and television, spent a year firing off more than 2,800 applications. Interviews: fewer than twenty. Jobs: none. She says she is close to a nervous collapse.
Once she was selective—only roles that matched her major. Then she learned that selectivity changed nothing, so she applied to everything. By the end, every time her phone lit up, her heart sank first: another rejection, or a message that had nothing to do with her.
This year 12.7 million new graduates are all shoving toward the same exit. In July the urban unemployment rate for 16-to-24-year-olds, students excluded, reached 17.9 percent. The figure looks weightless on the page. On a graduate’s chest it sits like a millstone.
Fresh graduates used to learn the craft on entry-level work: clerking, drafting copy, doing the prep, sketching, translating, writing basic code. Now they are crushed from both ends. Too many bodies on one side; on the other, artificial intelligence has simply taken the starter jobs.
No experience, you cannot get in. Cannot get in, you never get experience. A boss in Hangzhou put it without ornament: there are too many people. We need someone who can work tomorrow. We have no interest in training novices.
The door was not locked. It was bricked shut.
Some still treat “unemployed upon graduation” as the online self-pity of a few. The cruelty is that it is a live nerve, cutting through thousands of households.
To survive, many university graduates now deliver takeout. Some, to survive, have sold their bodies as well. Men and women both.
In Old Deng’s time the country was poor, but once you passed the university exam you had, in effect, an iron rice bowl. Most families did not have to smash the pot to send a child to school. The poorest even received a living stipend from the institution. I lived on that stipend all the way through my doctorate.
We were poor as students—poor enough that inviting a girl you liked to a twenty-cent film on the weekend required real calculation. But there was no dread hanging over the years of study, because graduation meant assignment: every graduate was guaranteed work. No one left campus unemployed. And the moment you started, you received the treatment of a state cadre; even if you came from a village, you immediately received an urban hukou.
The country was truly poor then. Yet you could go home and say to your parents, with pride: I have a job. I can begin to repay what you gave me.
Now the country is the world’s second-largest economy, and graduates stay up all night refreshing job apps, scatter résumés in every direction, and cannot even land a decent interview.
When the nation was poor it could still give every graduate work. Why, once it grew rich, can it no longer hold them? It is not that there is no money. It is that those in office no longer regard the children of ordinary people as human. Ordinary people are numbers on a spreadsheet, risks on a stability-maintenance list, interchangeable labor—not citizens whose livelihoods must be secured.
China has never lacked work that needs doing. In almost every major city a heavy rain turns streets into lakes. In some places people die. Even the capital can drown dozens in a single downpour.
For thirty years, unscrupulous developers chased quick money: buildings shot up above ground while the pipes below were never built to code at the same time. Above ground: political achievement. Below ground: unpaid debt. That debt is collected every year now—in ordinary lives, and in homes rotting under floodwater.
These repairs should have begun long ago: pipes, drainage, pumping stations, roads, the missing networks under old neighborhoods. Estimates say that once the work is fully launched it could absorb at least twenty million jobs a year and lift the whole economy with it. And every one of those jobs requires a human body. Artificial intelligence cannot do them.
Inside the country there is no shortage of such projects—work that already threatens lives and urgently needs doing. Look at the thousands of reservoirs and power stations that could kill hundreds or thousands at any moment, that have already killed many this year, that could burst at any time. Start any one of those restorations and you create tens of thousands of posts that no algorithm can replace.
On one side, young people cannot find work. On the other, a rainstorm and the reservoir fails, people die, the city becomes a swamp. It is not that there is no work. It is that the work that must be done is deliberately left undone, so that a few can keep making dirty money and keep building façades.
Two thousand eight hundred résumés. It is not that she did not try. It is that certain people never gave the young a chance to try.
When the pocket is empty, the family can still share another mouthful of rice. When the person is hollowed out, that is the real end.
When the young no longer dare speak of serving their parents or serving the country; when they reach the consensus that effort does not matter, that what matters is the bloodline you came from and the genitals you were born with—then this society is nearly finished.
A diploma can be locked in a drawer. Treating people as people cannot be locked away any longer.
In truth, even if they wanted to lock it, they could not.
Unemployed the day you graduate. Dead the day it rains. In the end it will turn and devour those who set it in motion.
An age that refuses to treat people as human, yet still demands their gratitude? There is no such door.

text:
题目：
投了2800份简历，面试不到20场，录取为零。
广播电视专业的硕士周津妮亚，一年时间投了两千八百多份简历，面试不到二十次，到现在一份工作都没拿到。她自己说：精神几近崩溃！
以前她还挑工作，专业对口才投。后来发现挑不挑一个样，就开始什么都投。投到最后，手机一亮，心先凉半截：不是拒绝就是无关消息。
今年有一千二百七十万应届生一起往外挤。七月，十六到二十四岁、不含在校生的城镇失业率到了百分之十七点九。数字看着轻飘飘，但在毕业生的心上，却像千斤重的巨石一般。
本来刚毕业的人，先要靠那些入门工作练手：文员、写材料、做前期、画草图、翻译、写点基础代码。但现在是两头堵。一边是人多得溢出，一边是人工智能把这些下手活直接做了。
你没经验，进不去；进不去，就永远没经验。杭州那边老板说得更直接：人太多了，我们要马上就能干活的，没兴趣培养新手。
门不是被锁上了，是直接被砌成了墙。
有人觉得“毕业即失业”只是网上某些人的无病呻吟，但可悲的是，这是正在发生的刺痛着千家万户的现实。
为了生存，很多大学毕业生不得不去送外卖。而有些人为了生存，不得不连自己的身体也一起出卖了。男女都有。
老邓那个时候，虽然国家也很穷，但只要考上大学，基本就等于端上铁饭碗。
大多数大学生读书，家里不用砸锅卖铁。家里生活特别困难的，学校还倒过来发点生活费。我就是靠学校发的生活费一直读到了博士毕业。
虽然当学生时的确很穷，穷到连想邀请喜欢的女同学周末看场两毛钱一场的电影都需要好好掂量。但那时上学还真没有任何后顾之忧，因为毕业包分配，保证每个毕业生都会有一份工作。没有任何一个人会一毕业就失业。而且一参加工作就享受国家干部待遇，即便来自农村，也马上能拿到城市户口。
那时候是真穷，可你回到家，仍可以很自豪地对父母说：我有工作了，我现在可以报答父母的养育之恩了。
现在国家已经富到世界第二大经济体了，但毕业生们却要熬夜刷招聘软件，广投简历，却连像样的面试都等不到。
国家穷的时候尚能让每个毕业生都有工作，为什么富了以后反而托不住了呢？不是没钱，是当官的不再把老百姓的孩子当人看了。老百姓只是报表上的数字，是维稳名单上的隐患，是随时可以换掉的劳力，不是必须解决他们生计的公民。
其实中国从来就不缺少工作岗位。现在中国几乎所有大城市，一场大雨就能积水成灾。有的地方直接死人，连首都一场大雨也能淹死几十人。
这三十年来，黑心房地产商为了赚快钱，地面楼盖得飞快，地下的管网根本没按规定同时修好。地上是政绩，地下是欠账。这账现在年年都要还，还的是普通百姓的命，还有被水泡烂的家。
这些修复工程早该全面开工：修管子、修排水、修泵站、修路、把老小区地下那些该补上的管网全部补上。据推算，工程一旦铺开，每年至少能消化两千万人就业，整体经济也能同时被带活起来。而且这些活全得真人去干，人工智能代替不了。
其实在中国境内，像这样严重威胁人民群众生命安全急需维护的工程比比皆是。你看那数以千计随时可能成百上千杀人、今年也已经杀了很多人、随时可能决堤的水库电站，哪一样修复工程开工都可以提供数以万计、人工智能绝对无法替代的工作岗位。
一边是年轻人找不到工作，一边是一下雨水库就决堤死人、城市就变泽国的惨剧。不是没有工作。是该干的活有人故意不让干，好让少数人继续赚昧心钱，继续搞面子工程。
两千八百份简历，不是她不努力，是某些人根本就不给年轻人努力的机会。
口袋空了，家里或许还能再匀一口饭。人被掏空，才真正完了！
当年轻人不敢再谈报效父母、报效国家时，当年轻人形成共识认为，努力不努力并不重要，重要的是你来自于那种血缘和生殖器时，这个社会也就快完了！
毕业证可以锁进抽屉，但把人当人这事却不能再锁了！
其实就是想锁也锁不了！
一毕业就失业，一下雨就死人，最终会反噬始作俑者的！
不把人当人，还要人去感谢你的时代，没门！

text:
Vperyod, Rossiya!LESSONS FOR AFRICA: SOVEREIGNTY IS DEFENDED & NOT NEGOTIATED 

Rozvi-Changamire 

Vperyod, Rossiya!; Forward, Russia!@RussiaIsntEnemy 

When this rallying cry rings out across the vast Russian steppes, it carries a weight that reaches far beyond the borders of Eastern Europe. It isn't just a patriotic phrase; it is an uncompromising declaration of national survival; a defiance against bending the knee to foreign pressure. Look past the standard Western media narratives surrounding the war in Ukraine, and a much bigger geopolitical reality comes into focus. 

Russia’s decision to draw a hard line against NATO’s eastward expansion isn't simply a local conflict. It’s an aggressive assertion of national security. For an African continent that is still wrestling with the subtle, persistent grip of foreign interference, Russia's refusal to back down holds a lesson that cannot be ignored; a lesson that real sovereignty isn't handed out at a negotiation table; it has to be claimed and fiercely defended.

This connection between Moscow and Africa isn't new; it has deep historical roots. Cast your mind back to the Soviet era, when Russia operated under a Marxist, socialist framework. That state-centered model, rooted in collective survival and state-guided development, struck an immediate chord with Africa’s own traditional philosophies, concepts like Hunhu/Ubuntu in Southern Africa or Ujamaa in East Africa.

When African movements took up arms to break free from European colonial rule, it was the Soviet Union that stepped in with weapons, training, and political backing. Crucially, Russia never colonized a single square inch of African land. Its history across the continent remains untainted by the brutal scramble and extraction that defined Western rule, reflecting a fundamental respect for territorial integrity that aligns naturally with Africa’s own liberation ideals.

Yet, decades after those colonial flags were lowered, much of Africa remains locked in a subtle form of economic servitude. While individual nations fly their own flags and host independence day parades, the continent as a whole has struggled to present a united front capable of protecting its own wealth. Western powers and foreign corporations still extract African gold, coltan, crude oil, and lithium under lopsided contracts. Meanwhile, some Africans are often tangled in corruption or beholden to foreign patrons, end up serving outside interests instead of safeguarding their own people's future.

This is precisely why Russia’s current posture offers such a compelling case study. Hit with an unprecedented wave of Western sanctions, asset freezes, and proxy military force, Moscow didn't collapse. Instead, it doubled down on its domestic economy, secured its resource pipelines, and proved that a state willing to stand its ground can weather immense international pressure. It served as a reminder that true independence requires zero tolerance for foreign economic or military coercion.

Africa needs to shed the posture of passive compliance. If African states genuinely want to break free from the cycle of exploitation, they have to study this kind of strategic resilience. That means building real, collective defense structures, taking absolute control over natural resources, and shutting the door on foreign control. In a world shaped by raw power, survival belongs only to those who protect their borders and assets without apology.

The time has come for the continent to wake up, secure its riches, and carve out a future on its own terms. To finally break the chains of neocolonial control, Africa would do well to adopt that very same spirit of unyielding forward momentum. "Vperyod, Rossiya!"; Forward, Russia!

text:
💔 DEVASTATING: A Mom Fighting Cancer Just Wanted Help. 
Now Her Sitter Won’t Return the Family Puppy.
Hanna Bustos, a Miami mom of five undergoing chemotherapy, is living a nightmare. In 2025, a local dog boarder offered to temporarily watch the family’s 1-year-old poodle, Lucy, for free to ease the burden of Hanna's cancer treatments.
But when Hanna asked for Lucy back, the sitter flatly refused.
Her reason? 
She text-messaged Hanna saying she didn't want to "remove Lucy from her pack," adding,
"I am very sorry you are going through this, but this doesn't change my decision. I am not giving her up."
Hanna’s 14-year-old son is completely heartbroken Lucy is his best friend. 
Because the arrangement was verbal and over text, police say it’s a civil matter. The family has now hired a lawyer and launched a campaign to fight back.
Let's help get the word out for this family. A dog belongs with the family who loves her.

text:
Conservative Perspective on City Policies and Jewish State Legitimacy

From a conservative viewpoint, Zohran Mamdani’s actions and plans as New York City mayor are not just isolated measures aimed at affordability. Instead, they represent a consistent pattern of increasing government influence over private markets, property, and prices, while also viewing the Jewish state as uniquely illegitimate. Conservatives believe this approach does two things simultaneously: it makes the language and methods of socialism seem normal and acceptable, and it erodes the cultural and institutional defenses that have traditionally protected American Jews.

Economic policies as incremental socialism

Mamdani, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, has stated that socialists should keep working toward seizing the means of production, even if it isn't currently popular. He also argues that worker ownership of production is essential for full economic participation. Conservatives interpret this language as more than just youthful rhetoric; they view it as indicative of his actual policy goals.

City-owned grocery stores are the most visible example. The proposal uses public buildings, tax exemptions, and wholesale purchasing so the government can undercut private retailers. Critics compare this to state grocery operations in socialist systems that produced shortages, low quality, and political allocation of food rather than market signals. Even a pilot program, they argue, establishes the principle that the state should compete with—and eventually crowd out—private enterprise in a basic consumer good.

Rent freezes for many stabilized units, along with large-scale publicly owned or financed social housing, amount to government price controls in the housing market. Conservatives argue that rent control often decreases supply, discourages maintenance, and shifts power from owners to political bodies. Increasing public ownership of housing takes the city further from a private-property system toward the social-housing model exemplified by Vienna, as Mamdani noted. When combined with proposals to seize neglected private buildings, it appears to form a ratchet: first freeze prices, then expand public housing, and finally absorb struggling private stock.

The funding approach—raising corporate taxes and imposing a surcharge on millionaires—operates on the same principle. Conservatives see steep, targeted tax hikes on capital and high earners as class warfare that penalizes the mobile tax base that New York already finds hard to keep. Once government programs are established and the private sector faces pressure, the demand for more state control increases. Initiatives like free buses, universal childcare, and a $30 minimum wage form a broader picture of an expanding public sector that replaces market-driven prices and contracts with political decisions. Each measure can be justified as making life more affordable, but together they shift the default from private markets to government provision.

The slippery-slope argument is rooted in history, not conspiracy: when the state takes control as the main landlord, grocer, and wage-setter in a large American city, support for further nationalization increases while demand for market discipline declines. Conservatives highlight how other cities and countries, which initially implemented “democratic” price controls and public enterprises, eventually faced persistent shortages and capital leaving.

Israel policy and the antisemitism concern

Conservatives addressing the Jewish question note that New York City has the largest Jewish population outside Israel, and antisemitic incidents increased significantly after October 7, 2023. In this context, a mayor who labels Israel as an apartheid or genocidal state, supports BDS, and refuses to acknowledge Israel’s identity as a Jewish state is not merely expressing a foreign-policy opinion. Instead, he is applying a distinct standard to the world’s only Jewish-majority nation.

Mamdani supports BDS, has called Israel an apartheid state, and used the term “genocide” for the Gaza conflict. He advocates for Israel to be a state with equal rights, not exclusively Jewish. He expressed discomfort with any nation that establishes a citizenship hierarchy based on religion. Many conservatives and mainstream Jewish groups see denying Jewish self-determination—while accepting other ethnic and religious states—as a major form of antisemitism today. The IHRA working definition, which Mamdani’s administration chose not to keep, explicitly lists “denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination” as antisemitism. Removing this definition and the anti-BDS contract rule on the first day was seen as eliminating tools to differentiate legitimate criticism from delegitimization.

The appointment of officials with documented connections to groups like Students for Justice in Palestine, Jewish Voice for Peace, and Within Our Lifetime raises concerns. These organizations have a history of rhetoric and protests that many Jews find hostile, such as chants and symbols linked to Hamas. Conservatives contend that when city government presents anti-Zionism as the acceptable default, it diminishes the social consequences of more blatant antisemitic actions. Mamdani's distinction—“I criticize the Israeli government, not Jews”—is seen as inadequate when criticisms target only the Jewish state and the activist environment routinely blurs the line between the two.

The main concern is the spread of cultural and political influence. If the largest U.S. city mainstreams BDS and opposes Jewish self-determination, similar rhetoric may become common in universities, unions, and other Democratic strongholds. Conservatives view this as a gradual process: initially isolating Israel, then questioning Jewish ties to it, which leads to increased antisemitic incidents. Officials often claim they are merely discussing "policy," despite the rising incidents.

From a conservative standpoint, Mamdani's behavior fits a pattern of recurring tendencies within socialist movements: viewing private ownership as problematic, trusting ideology over markets or current social systems, and treating organized movements as the primary agents of history. Conservatives contend that Mamdani’s history exemplifies these tendencies in a democratic, local context.

Shared ideological vocabulary

Mamdani adopts language rooted in the Marxist tradition, rather than the New Deal or Nordic social democratic approaches. In 2021, he told Young Democratic Socialists that BDS and “the end goal of seizing the means of production” are principles “we firmly believe in,” despite lacking majority support. He emphasized that organizers should pursue both popular demands and the unpopular end goal “in tandem.” In 2020, he shared a variation of Marx’s phrase: “Each according to their need, each according to their ability.” He has stated that billionaires should not exist and advocates for worker ownership of the means of production to ensure full economic participation. During his inauguration, he vowed to replace “the frigidity of rugged individualism with the warmth of collectivism.”

Conservatives interpret this as part of a series of ideas that span from Marx to Lenin’s nationalizations and Stalin’s command economy. The phrase "seizing the means of production” is not just a Scandinavian welfare slogan; it encapsulates Marx's fundamental belief that factories, land, and capital should transfer from private owners to collective or state control. Practices like city-owned grocery stores, public social housing, rent freezes, and political boards setting prices are seen as small-scale expressions of the same goal: replacing market-based allocation with political decision-making. Larry Kudlow and others have explicitly connected these ideas to Stalin, equating the confiscation of productive assets, whether through taxation, regulation, or public enterprise, with Stalin's policies.

Mamdani also highlighted a Communist Party of India (Marxist) mayor as an example of the type of leadership New York requires. He emphasized that DSA itself—not just individual voters—provides legitimacy, stating that elected socialists are “special because of our organization.” Conservatives view this as movement-first politics.

The party, the movement, and “conviction over calculus”

Stalin’s leadership exemplifies the extreme prioritization of the party over the people. Although the Bolsheviks professed to serve the working class, in reality, the Party determined what served the class’s interests. Democratic centralism required party unity following decisions. Terms like “Kulaks,” “wreckers,” and “right deviationists” were viewed not as fellow citizens with differing perspectives but as threats to the party line. This mindset led to policies involving famine, show trials, and a state that considered human suffering secondary to the Plan.

Conservatives do not assert that Mamdani has a secret police or famine policy. Instead, they argue it reflects a less extreme version of the same underlying priorities.

The conservative comparison with Stalin focuses on who decides the common good. In Stalin's case, the Party decided. Mamdani's description suggests that a socialist body establishes meanings for concepts like 'working people,” “dignity,” and “what is correct,” then offers these definitions to citizens through services such as childcare, transportation, and housing. While the public can express their views, they do not ultimately determine the final decision.

Historical rhymes conservatives emphasize

Lenin: Popular demands come first, followed by the actual program. Dual power and “who whom.” Conservatives interpret Mamdani’s 2021 speech—highlighting Medicare for All and debt cancellation, while maintaining focus on controlling production and BDS—as a small-scale version of that sequence.

Stalin: Classifies enemies as a category of governance. Conservatives argue that rhetoric against landlords, corporations, and billionaires, along with administrative measures like rent boards, tax lists, and public takeovers of neglected buildings, serve as a legalistic way of labeling a disliked economic class. A Washington Examiner article even likened Mamdani's pied-à-terre tax list to traditional practices of targeting a specific class—not as a threat of violence, but as a caution about stigmatizing citizens based on economic status.

Chávez and Maduro: Price controls, state-led grocery programs, housing promises, and slogans like “the people versus the oligarchy” have been followed by shortages and capital flight. Mamdani views city grocery pilot projects and rent freezes as the beginning of this ongoing narrative, not its conclusion.

Castro’s early phase: Reject the communist label, position as a reformer, and maintain the movement’s ultimate goal. Mamdani consistently states he is not a communist. Conservatives argue that the label matters less than the actual program and language used, noting that many socialists in the 20th century expressed similar sentiments during their rise.

“Sewer socialists” and Debs versus the revolutionary line: Mamdani frequently references Debs, La Guardia, and Milwaukee sewer socialists. Conservatives respond that those figures did not advocate seizing the means of production as an ultimate goal. They also argue that DSA’s wider alliances—such as BDS, opposition to NATO, and friendly relations with regimes like Cuba and Venezuela—align more with the Third World socialist tradition than with municipal pragmatism.

Mamdani faces conservative criticism for upholding ideas like prioritizing the collective over the individual, advocating political allocation over market-driven prices, focusing on movement conviction rather than popular support, and applying Islamo-Marxist and antisemitic standards to Jews and the Jewish state. These beliefs are part of a thought tradition that, if unchecked, can lead to regimes that favor party loyalty over the people's needs. Although New York’s safeguards may be effective, the real risk is that they do not reflect the underlying ideology. The primary concern remains Mamdani's stated ultimate goal.

In summary, critics argue that Mamdani’s economic plan views private property and markets as issues to be controlled or replaced by the state. Similarly, his Israel plan considers Jewish self-determination as a problem to be managed or substituted by a binational or “equal rights” approach. Both, they say, deviate from the liberal-democratic framework that has supported the growth of American Jews and capitalism. According to this perspective, whether the ultimate goal is full communism or just a tougher environment for Jews, it makes little difference once the process has started.

text:
Thomas Barrack and Split Vision
 Dr. Yahya Alaridi 
Part 2
The authorities possess the force. They possess the institutions. They claim to be the state. Therefore, they must provide evidence that they came to protect, not subjugate; to build a state, not reproduce the logic of domination.

Instead, they continue a policy of repression and criminality, shelling civilians, besieging them, and inciting against them.

The question therefore becomes clearer: Is Suwayda expected to place its trust in an authority that has offered no evidence that it is either capable of, or willing to, protect those who are supposedly its own citizens?

If Washington is serious about its repeated commitment to Syrian unity, it must understand that unity cannot be measured by the ability of an armed authority to impose its will on the country’s periphery.

A map is not a state. Control is not sovereignty. Subjugation is not national unity.

A state that needs force to keep its constituent communities within it has not solved the problem of division. It has merely postponed the explosion.

Unity built on fear is not unity. It is a ceasefire waiting to break.

Barrack has spoken of the death of the Sykes–Picot order. Yet the irony is that attempting to reimpose Damascus-centered rule by force may, in practice, reproduce the very logic of that era: borders and maps unified from the outside, while societies remain unreconciled within.

If Sykes–Picot has truly died, the lesson is not to return to an even more rigid centralism. It is to recognize that the future of the region will not be shaped by borders alone, but by legitimacy, security, and the ability to protect the communities that make up the state.

Suwayda is not a local detail that can be reduced to a single incident, a single person, or a political statement.

Its geographic, historical, political, and spiritual position at the heart of the Syrian-Lebanese-Jordanian triangle, and its direct proximity to Israel, make its security part of a broader regional security equation.

Anyone who genuinely seeks peace in the Levant cannot build it by ignoring the south or attempting to break the will of its people.

Peace built upon Suwayda’s fear will not be peace. It will be a truce awaiting the next round.

That is why the real question that should be put to Thomas Barrack is not: Why did you see one particular person?

It is: Why did you see him, but fail to see Suwayda?

Why did he appear so prominently in your account while thousands of besieged civilians disappeared from view?

Why did one incident appear while repeated violations vanished?

And why did the authorities’ narrative become so clearly visible, while the suffering of civilians remained outside the frame?

When this happens, the diplomat, knowingly or unknowingly, becomes more than a transmitter of a narrative. He becomes part of its production and entrenchment.

That is precisely what Washington should guard against.

The most dangerous thing a great power can do is not simply to mischaracterize an incident. It is to adopt the narrative of one party to a conflict and then use its political and international weight to elevate that narrative into truth.

If the American message to Damascus is that Syria must remain united, then let the message be clear:

Yes—but not at the expense of those who insist on their dignity; not through siege, not through shelling, not by ignoring violations, and not by turning victims into a footnote in the authorities’ narrative.

The unity of Syria cannot be a project for subjugating Syrians. A state cannot be built by forcing its constituent communities to submit. It is built by convincing them that the state has come to protect them, not to kill them.

text:
I am not so sure there is anything Canada should not be willing to concede in order to reduce or eliminate US tariffs.

That's my opinion.  Almost all the things that the Liberals want to protect, I would want to eliminate tomorrow.

Of all the irritants the Americans have listed, I am not so sure there is a single one of them that I would not eliminate.  Most of them exist to protect against American competition.

Of course, like any good negotiator I would not let the Americans know that, and I would only hand over what is necessary, and only if I got something in return.  I'd be coy about it.

However, in my mind I would not care about eliminating any of them.

Eliminating them might produce short-term economic harm, but long-term economic gain.  The short-term harm would only occur because of how uncompetitive the companies that they protect have become.

As for "we risk giving Washington a remarkably easy negotiating position: almost any demand can be excused by saying Canada brought it on itself."  - that makes no sense to me.

I don't see how that affects negotiations at all.  It doesn't matter why something exists.  All that matters is what you are willing to offer and what you are demanding in return.  "why" something exists has no bearing, it doesn't matter whether Canada brought something on itself, or whether it exists for other reasons.
